sections.title: Deriving the six equations of motion
Deriving the six equations of motion

inlines.text: The three equations of motion in one dimension describe
In projectile motion, there are six equations of motion:
three for horizontal motion and three for vertical motion.
Every projectile motion problem starts from two facts:
No horizontal force acts, so there is no horizontal acceleration.
The only vertical force is the constant force of gravity.
The remaining four equations follow by integrating these twice.

content.prompt:
A ball is thrown from the origin with speed $40\text{ m/s}$ at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal.
Taking $g=10\text{ m/s}^2$, derive the six equations of motion.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}&=\int 0\,dt\\\dot{x}&=C_1\\\dot{x}(0)&=40\cos30^\circ\\\dot{x}(0)&=20\sqrt{3}\\C_1&=20\sqrt{3}\\\dot{x}&=20\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int20\sqrt{3}\,dt\\x&=20\sqrt{3}t+C_2\\x(0)&=0\\0&=20\sqrt{3}(0)+C_2\\C_2&=0\\x&=20\sqrt{3}t\end{aligned}$$

You are expected to derive the six equations, unless given to you in a question.
Memorising them alone is not enough in an exam, as there will be marks for the derivation.
In the next few sections of the booklet, we will skip the derivation to save time.
The six equations above give the scalar components for each direction.
We can combine them into vector form for acceleration, velocity, and displacement:
Write these components as a vector.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{v}&=\dot{x}\mathbf{i}+\dot{y}\mathbf{j}\\\underset{\sim}{v}&=20\mathbf{i}+(-10t+20)\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{r}&=x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j}\\\underset{\sim}{r}&=20t\mathbf{i}+(-5t^2+20t)\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt:
A ball is thrown from the origin with speed $40$ m/s at $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)$ above the horizontal. Take $g=10$ m/s².

Derive the six equations and write $\mathbf r$ in vector form.

answer.short:
$a_x=0$, $a_y=-10$, $v_x=32$, $v_y=24-10t$, $x=32t$, $y=24t-5t^2$.

$\mathbf r=32t\mathbf i+(24t-5t^2)\mathbf j$ m, with $t$ in seconds.
answer.worked:
Take the launch point as the origin, with upward positive. Acceleration is in m/s², velocity in m/s and displacement in metres.

$$\begin{aligned}\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac34\right)\\ \sin\theta&=\frac35\\ \cos\theta&=\frac45\\ u_x&=40\cos\theta=40\cdot\frac45=32\\ u_y&=40\sin\theta=40\cdot\frac35=24\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}a_x&=0\\ a_y&=-10\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dv_x}{dt}&=0\\ v_x&=C_1\\ v_x(0)&=32\\ C_1&=32\\ \boxed{v_x=32}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dv_y}{dt}&=-10\\ v_y&=-10t+C_2\\ v_y(0)&=24\\ C_2&=24\\ \boxed{v_y=24-10t}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dx}{dt}&=v_x=32\\ x&=32t+C_3\\ x(0)&=0\\ C_3&=0\\ \boxed{x=32t}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dt}&=v_y=24-10t\\ y&=24t-5t^2+C_4\\ y(0)&=0\\ C_4&=0\\ \boxed{y=24t-5t^2}\end{aligned}$$

$$\boxed{\mathbf r=32t\mathbf i+(24t-5t^2)\mathbf j}$$

content.prompt:
A particle is projected from the origin with speed $V$ at angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. By integrating, show that

$$\mathbf v=(V\cos\theta)\mathbf i+(-10t+V\sin\theta)\mathbf j$$

and

$$\mathbf r=(Vt\cos\theta)\mathbf i+(-5t^2+Vt\sin\theta)\mathbf j.$$

Take $g=10$ m/s².

answer.short: $\mathbf v=(V\cos\theta)\mathbf i+(-10t+V\sin\theta)\mathbf j$ and $\mathbf r=(Vt\cos\theta)\mathbf i+(-5t^2+Vt\sin\theta)\mathbf j$, obtained by integrating $\mathbf a=-10\mathbf j$ and using the initial velocity and $\mathbf r(0)=\mathbf0$.
answer.worked:
$$\mathbf a=0\mathbf i-10\mathbf j$$

$$\begin{aligned}\mathbf v&=\int(0\mathbf i-10\mathbf j)\,dt\\ \mathbf v&=C_1\mathbf i+(-10t+C_2)\mathbf j\\ \mathbf v(0)&=V\cos\theta\mathbf i+V\sin\theta\mathbf j\\ C_1&=V\cos\theta\\ C_2&=V\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$

$$\boxed{\mathbf v=(V\cos\theta)\mathbf i+(-10t+V\sin\theta)\mathbf j}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\mathbf r&=\int\left[(V\cos\theta)\mathbf i+(-10t+V\sin\theta)\mathbf j\right]dt\\ \mathbf r&=(Vt\cos\theta+C_3)\mathbf i\\ &\quad+(-5t^2+Vt\sin\theta+C_4)\mathbf j\\ \mathbf r(0)&=0\mathbf i+0\mathbf j\\ C_3&=0\\ C_4&=0\end{aligned}$$

$$\boxed{\mathbf r=(Vt\cos\theta)\mathbf i+(-5t^2+Vt\sin\theta)\mathbf j}$$

Here $t$ is in seconds, $V$ and $\mathbf v$ are in m/s, and $\mathbf r$ is in metres.

Decide which equation to use to find each of these quantities.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find horizontal displacement at $t=3$

answer.worked: Use the horizontal displacement equation and evaluate $x(3)$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the time to reach maximum height

answer.worked: At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero. Solve $\dot y(t)=0$ for $t$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the time of flight

answer.short: Solve $y(t)=0$ and choose the positive landing time.
answer.worked: For the ground-level launch described in the teaching, solve $y(t)=0$. Exclude $t=0$, the launch time, and choose the positive landing time.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the maximum height

answer.short: Solve $\dot y(t)=0$, then substitute that time into $y(t)$.
answer.worked: Solve $\dot y(t)=0$ to find $t_{y\max}$. The maximum height is $y(t_{y\max})$.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Find the horizontal velocity at $t=3$

answer.worked: Use the horizontal velocity equation and evaluate $\dot x(3)$.

children.label: f
children.prompt: Find the time when the projectile is 15 m above the ground.

answer.worked: With ground level given by $y=0$, solve $y(t)=15$ for the time or times during flight.

children.label: g
children.prompt: Find the range

answer.short: Find the positive landing time from $y(t)=0$, then substitute into $x(t)$.
answer.worked: Solve $y(t)=0$ for the positive landing time $t_{\mathrm{flight}}$. The range is $x(t_{\mathrm{flight}})$.

children.label: h
children.prompt: Find the speed when the projectile lands

answer.short: Find the landing time $T$, then evaluate $\sqrt{[\dot x(T)]^2+[\dot y(T)]^2}$.
answer.worked:
Solve $y(t)=0$ for the positive landing time $T$. Evaluate both velocity components at $T$, then use
$$v=\sqrt{[\dot x(T)]^2+[\dot y(T)]^2}.$$

children.label: i
children.prompt: Find the angle at which the projectile lands

answer.short: Find the landing time $T$ and velocity components, then use $\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{|\dot y(T)|}{\dot x(T)}\right)$ below the horizontal.
answer.worked:
Solve $y(t)=0$ for the positive landing time $T$. Evaluate $\dot x(T)$ and $\dot y(T)$. For the rightward motion shown in the teaching,
$$\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{|\dot y(T)|}{\dot x(T)}\right).$$
The landing direction is $\theta$ below the horizontal.

children.label: j
children.prompt: Find when the horizontal displacement is 6 m from the origin

answer.worked: Use the horizontal displacement equation and solve $x(t)=6$ for $t$.

$t=0$ or $-5t+10\sqrt2=0$.

Therefore $t=0$ or $t=2\sqrt2\text{ s}$. The total time of flight is $2\sqrt2\text{ s}$.

Let $\theta=\tan^{-1}(\frac{4}{3})$. Then
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac43,\\\sin\theta&=\frac45,\qquad \cos\theta=\frac35.\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$\begin{align*}\dot{x}&=60\cos\theta\\&=60\left(\frac35\right)\\&=36,\\\dot{y}&=-10t+60\sin\theta\\&=-10t+60\left(\frac45\right)\\&=-10t+48.\end{align*}$$

At launch, $t=0$ and $x=y=0$, so $C_1=C_2=0$. Therefore
$$\begin{align*}x&=36t,\\y&=-5t^2+48t.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\dot{x}(3)&=36,\\\dot{y}(3)&=-10(3)+48\\&=18.\end{align*}$$
Thus the speed is
$$\begin{align*}V&=\sqrt{36^2+18^2}\\&=\sqrt{1620}\\&=18\sqrt5\text{ m/s}.\end{align*}$$
Both velocity components are positive, so the direction is above the horizontal:
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{18}{36}\right)\\&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac12\right).\end{align*}$$

spec.mathematics: For horizontal coordinate x, the paths are y=sqrt(3)x-x²/20 and y=x/sqrt(3)-x²/60, both ending at x=20sqrt(3).

children.label: a
children.prompt: Which stone finishes its flight first and by how long? Give the time difference exactly and to 1 d.p.

answer.short: The stone thrown at $30^\circ$ lands first, by $2\sqrt3-2\text{ s}\approx1.5\text{ s}$.
answer.worked:
For the stone thrown at $60^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned}x_1&=10t\\y_1&=10\sqrt3t-5t^2\end{aligned}$$
For the stone thrown at $30^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned}x_2&=10\sqrt3t\\y_2&=10t-5t^2\end{aligned}$$
Set each vertical displacement to zero and take the positive time.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=t(10\sqrt3-5t)\\t_1&=2\sqrt3\text{ s}\\0&=t(10-5t)\\t_2&=2\text{ s}\\t_1-t_2&=2\sqrt3-2\text{ s}\\&\approx1.5\text{ s}\end{aligned}$$
The stone thrown at $30^\circ$ lands first.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the 2 stones land at the same place.

answer.short: Both land $20\sqrt3\text{ m}$ from the common launch point.
answer.worked:
Substitute each positive landing time into its horizontal displacement equation.
$$\begin{aligned}x_1(2\sqrt3)&=10(2\sqrt3)\\&=20\sqrt3\text{ m}\\x_2(2)&=10\sqrt3(2)\\&=20\sqrt3\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
Both stones start at the same point and travel in the same horizontal direction, so they land at the same place.

content.prompt: A ball is thrown at $15\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $60^\circ$. At the same time another ball is thrown from a point $30\text{ m}$ away, back towards the first, at $45^\circ$ and $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$. How far apart do they land? Give your answer to 1 d.p. Use $g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

spec.description: Oppositely directed launches, crossing trajectories, speed and angle labels, and a dimension between launch points. Paths are plotted from the given equations; the second ball's apex is consequently slightly higher than the first, correcting the source schematic.
spec.mathematics: First trajectory y=sqrt(3)x-4x²/45 for 0≤x≤225sqrt(3)/20. Second trajectory y=(30-x)-(30-x)²/40 for -10≤x≤30. Launch points are x=0 and x=30.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied question figure without calculated landing coordinates or separation.

answer.worked:
Take the first launch point as $x=0$, with positive $x$ towards the second launch point.
For ball 1:
$$\begin{aligned}y_1&=15t\sin60^\circ-5t^2\\0&=t\left(\frac{15\sqrt3}{2}-5t\right)\\t_1&=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}\text{ s}\\x_1&=15\cos60^\circ\left(\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}\right)\\&=\frac{45\sqrt3}{4}\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
For ball 2, the horizontal velocity is negative:
$$\begin{aligned}y_2&=20t\sin45^\circ-5t^2\\0&=t(10\sqrt2-5t)\\t_2&=2\sqrt2\text{ s}\\x_2&=30-20\cos45^\circ(2\sqrt2)\\&=30-40\\&=-10\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
The distance between the landing points is
$$\begin{aligned}d&=\frac{45\sqrt3}{4}-(-10)\\&=10+\frac{45\sqrt3}{4}\\&\approx29.5\text{ m}.\end{aligned}$$

children.prompt:
A ball is thrown from the top of a 40 m building at 15 m/s at $60^\circ$ above the horizontal.

Find the time to hit the ground, range, and maximum height to 1 d.p.

spec.description: Illustrative upright building, ball at its top, and dashed trajectory rising to a maximum before reaching ground to the right. No printed measurements or labels. Ordinary trajectory changed from decorative source blue to house black.
spec.mathematics: Launch above ground with positive initial vertical velocity; one maximum followed by ground impact. Diagram is illustrative, not to scale.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent question diagram; no answers.

answer.short: Time of flight: $4.4\text{ s}$; range: $33.1\text{ m}$; maximum height above ground: $48.4\text{ m}$.
answer.worked:
Take the launch point as the origin, so ground level is $y=-40$.

$$\begin{aligned}
\dot{x}&=15\cos60^\circ=\frac{15}{2},\\
\dot{y}&=-10t+\frac{15\sqrt3}{2},\\
x&=\frac{15}{2}t,\\
y&=-5t^2+\frac{15\sqrt3}{2}t.
\end{aligned}$$
At ground impact:
$$\begin{aligned}
-40&=-5t^2+\frac{15\sqrt3}{2}t,\\
10t^2-15\sqrt3\,t-80&=0,\\
t&=\frac{3\sqrt3+\sqrt{155}}{4}\\
&\approx4.4\text{ s}.
\end{aligned}$$
The negative root is rejected because $t\geq0$.
$$\begin{aligned}
R&=\frac{15}{2}\left(\frac{3\sqrt3+\sqrt{155}}{4}\right)\\
&\approx33.1\text{ m}.
\end{aligned}$$
At maximum height, $\dot y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}
0&=-10t+\frac{15\sqrt3}{2},\\
t&=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4},\\
y_{\max}&=-5\left(\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\right)^2+\frac{15\sqrt3}{2}\left(\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\right)\\
&=\frac{135}{16},\\
H_{\max}&=40+\frac{135}{16}\\
&\approx48.4\text{ m above ground}.
\end{aligned}$$

A ball is rolled off horizontally from the top of a 25 m cliff at 20 m/s.

answer.short: Time of flight: $2.2\text{ s}$; range: $44.7\text{ m}$; impact velocity: $30.0\text{ m/s}$ at $48.2^\circ$ below the horizontal.
answer.worked:
Take the launch point as the origin, so ground level is $y=-25$.

$$\begin{aligned}
x&=20t,\\
y&=-5t^2,\\
\dot{x}&=20,\\
\dot{y}&=-10t.
\end{aligned}$$
At ground impact:
$$\begin{aligned}
-25&=-5t^2,\\
t&=\sqrt5\\
&\approx2.2\text{ s},\\
R&=20\sqrt5\\
&\approx44.7\text{ m}.
\end{aligned}$$
The impact velocity components are $20\text{ m/s}$ horizontally and $-10\sqrt5\text{ m/s}$ vertically.
$$\begin{aligned}
v&=\sqrt{20^2+(-10\sqrt5)^2}\\
&=30.0\text{ m/s},\\
\alpha&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{10\sqrt5}{20}\right)\\
&\approx48.2^\circ.
\end{aligned}$$
The impact velocity is $30.0\text{ m/s}$ at $48.2^\circ$ below the horizontal.

children.prompt:
A ball is thrown from the top of a 20 m cliff at 10 m/s at $30^\circ$ below the horizontal.

Find its velocity when the ball is 5 m above the ground to 1 d.p.

spec.description: Illustrative cliff representation with ball at its top, ground extending on both sides, and a dashed trajectory descending immediately to the right. No printed target-height, angle or measurement labels. Decorative source blue changed to house black.
spec.mathematics: Launch above ground with negative initial vertical velocity and downward acceleration. Diagram is illustrative, not to scale.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent question diagram; no answers.

answer.worked:
Take the launch point as the origin. At 5 m above ground, $y=5-20=-15$.

$$\begin{aligned}
\dot{x}&=10\cos30^\circ=5\sqrt3,\\
\dot{y}&=-10t-10\sin30^\circ=-10t-5,\\
y&=-5t^2-5t.
\end{aligned}$$
At the required height:
$$\begin{aligned}
-15&=-5t^2-5t,\\
t^2+t-3&=0,\\
t&=\frac{-1+\sqrt{13}}{2}.
\end{aligned}$$
The negative root is rejected because $t\geq0$.
$$\begin{aligned}
\dot{y}&=-10\left(\frac{-1+\sqrt{13}}{2}\right)-5\\
&=-5\sqrt{13},\\
v&=\sqrt{(5\sqrt3)^2+(-5\sqrt{13})^2}\\
&=20.0\text{ m/s},\\
\alpha&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{5\sqrt{13}}{5\sqrt3}\right)\\
&\approx64.3^\circ.
\end{aligned}$$
The velocity is $20.0\text{ m/s}$ at $64.3^\circ$ below the horizontal.

content.prompt: A horizontal drainpipe $6$ m above sea level empties storm water horizontally into the sea. The water reaches the sea $2$ m from the pipe. Find the initial speed to 1 d.p.

answer.worked:
Take the pipe as the origin, with upward positive. Since $\theta=0^\circ$,
$$y=-5t^2,\qquad x=Vt.$$
At sea level, $y=-6$:
$$\begin{align*}-5t^2&=-6\\t&=\sqrt{\frac65}\ \text{s}.\end{align*}$$
Using $x=2$:
$$\begin{align*}2&=V\sqrt{\frac65}\\V&=\frac{2}{\sqrt{6/5}}\\V&\approx1.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}\quad\text{(1 d.p.)}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A stone is thrown from the top of an $11\text{ m}$ high vertical tower.
The initial speed is $12\text{ m/s}$ and the initial direction is $30^\circ$ below the horizontal. Take $g=10\text{ m/s}^2$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Starting with the horizontal and vertical components of acceleration, show that $\dot{x}=6\sqrt{3}$ and $\dot{y}=-10t-6$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\ddot{x}&=0,\qquad \ddot{y}=-10\\\dot{x}&=C_1,\qquad \dot{y}=-10t+C_2\\\dot{x}(0)&=12\cos30^\circ=6\sqrt{3}\\\dot{y}(0)&=-12\sin30^\circ=-6\\\dot{x}&=6\sqrt{3}\\\dot{y}&=-10t-6\end{aligned}$$
The initial vertical velocity is negative because the stone is thrown downwards.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If the origin is at the point of projection, find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $t$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=6\sqrt{3}\,t+C_3\\y&=-5t^2-6t+C_4\end{aligned}$$
At the point of projection, $x(0)=y(0)=0$, so $C_3=C_4=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}x&=6\sqrt{3}\,t\\y&=-5t^2-6t\end{aligned}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: How long does it take for the stone to hit the ground?

answer.worked:
At ground level, $y=-11$.
$$\begin{aligned}-11&=-5t^2-6t\\5t^2+6t-11&=0\\(5t+11)(t-1)&=0\\t&=-\frac{11}{5}\quad\text{or}\quad t=1\end{aligned}$$
Reject the negative time. The stone hits the ground after $1\text{ s}$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: How far from the base of the tower does it land (to $1$ d.p.)?

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}x(1)&=6\sqrt{3}\times1\\&\approx10.4\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Show the stone hits the ground at an angle of $\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{8\sqrt{3}}{9}\right)$ below the horizontal.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}(1)&=6\sqrt{3}\\\dot{y}(1)&=-10-6=-16\\\tan\theta&=\frac{16}{6\sqrt{3}}\\&=\frac{8}{3\sqrt{3}}\\&=\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{9}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{9}\right)\end{aligned}$$
The vertical velocity is negative, so this angle is below the horizontal.

Taking the positive root gives $t\approx2.8\text{ s}$.

content.prompt:
Points $A$ and $B$ lie on a vertical line above the origin $O$ on the ground, with $OA=kh$ and $OB=h$, where $k>1$.

A particle is projected horizontally from $A$ with speed $U$. Some time later, a second particle is projected horizontally from $B$ with speed $V$. Both land at the same point on the ground.

Show that $\dfrac{V}{U}=\sqrt{k}$.

answer.worked:
Measure each flight time from that particle's launch.

For the particle launched from $A$:
$$\begin{aligned}x_A&=Ut,\\y_A&=kh-\frac12gt^2.\end{aligned}$$
At landing, $y_A=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=kh-\frac12gt^2,\\t&=\sqrt{\frac{2kh}{g}},\\x_A&=U\sqrt{\frac{2kh}{g}}.\end{aligned}$$
For the particle launched from $B$, let its flight time be $T$. At landing:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=h-\frac12gT^2,\\T&=\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}},\\x_B&=V\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}.\end{aligned}$$
The landing points are the same, so
$$\begin{aligned}U\sqrt{\frac{2kh}{g}}&=V\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}},\\\frac{V}{U}&=\frac{\sqrt{2kh/g}}{\sqrt{2h/g}},\\\frac{V}{U}&=\sqrt{k}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: The initial speed is $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the greatest height is $20\text{ m}$. Find $\alpha$ to the nearest degree.

answer.worked:
At the greatest height, $\dot y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}\dot y&=30\sin\alpha-10t\\0&=30\sin\alpha-10t\\t&=3\sin\alpha\end{align*}$$The height at this time is $20\text{ m}$.
$$\begin{align*}y&=-5t^2+30t\sin\alpha\\20&=-5(3\sin\alpha)^2+30\sin\alpha(3\sin\alpha)\\20&=-45\sin^2\alpha+90\sin^2\alpha\\\sin^2\alpha&=\frac49\\\sin\alpha&=\frac23\\\alpha&\approx42^\circ\end{align*}$$The angle of projection is acute.

children.label: b
children.prompt: The initial speed is $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the greatest height is $15\text{ m}$. Find $\alpha$ exactly.

answer.worked:
At the greatest height, $\dot y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}\dot y&=20\sin\alpha-10t\\0&=20\sin\alpha-10t\\t&=2\sin\alpha\end{align*}$$The height at this time is $15\text{ m}$.
$$\begin{align*}y&=-5t^2+20t\sin\alpha\\15&=-5(2\sin\alpha)^2+20\sin\alpha(2\sin\alpha)\\15&=-20\sin^2\alpha+40\sin^2\alpha\\\sin^2\alpha&=\frac34\\\sin\alpha&=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\\alpha&=60^\circ\end{align*}$$The angle of projection is acute.

answer.worked:

$$\begin{aligned}2000&=\frac V2t\\t&=\frac{4000}{V}.\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt:
A particle is projected from the origin at $30\text{ m/s}$ and passes through $(30,20)$.

It is given that
$$\underset{\sim}{r}=\begin{pmatrix}30\cos\theta\,t\\-5t^2+30\sin\theta\,t\end{pmatrix}.$$
Show that $\tan^2\theta-6\tan\theta+5=0$ and find both possible angles. Give non-exact angles to $1$ decimal place.

answer.worked:
From the horizontal equation,
$$\begin{align*}30&=30\cos\theta\,t\\t&=\frac{1}{\cos\theta}.\end{align*}$$
Substitute into the vertical equation with $y=20$:
$$\begin{align*}20&=30\sin\theta\left(\frac{1}{\cos\theta}\right)-5\left(\frac{1}{\cos\theta}\right)^2\\20&=30\tan\theta-5\sec^2\theta\\20&=30\tan\theta-5(1+\tan^2\theta)\\5\tan^2\theta-30\tan\theta+25&=0\\\tan^2\theta-6\tan\theta+5&=0\\(\tan\theta-1)(\tan\theta-5)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Hence $\tan\theta=1$ or $\tan\theta=5$, giving
$$\theta=45^\circ\quad\text{or}\quad\theta=\tan^{-1}(5)\approx78.7^\circ.$$

content.prompt: A particle is projected from the origin with initial speed $20\sqrt{2}$ m/s. On its flight it passes through the point $(20,15)$ at time $t$. Let $\theta$ be the angle of projection.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $\sqrt{2}t\cos\theta=1$ and $4\sqrt{2}t\sin\theta-t^2=3$.

answer.worked:
Using $g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}$,
$$\begin{aligned}x&=20\sqrt{2}t\cos\theta\\20&=20\sqrt{2}t\cos\theta\\\sqrt{2}t\cos\theta&=1.\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y&=-5t^2+20\sqrt{2}t\sin\theta\\15&=-5t^2+20\sqrt{2}t\sin\theta\\4\sqrt{2}t\sin\theta-t^2&=3.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence show that $\tan^2\theta-8\tan\theta+7=0$.

answer.worked:
From $\sqrt{2}t\cos\theta=1$,
$$t=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\cos\theta}.$$
Substitute into $4\sqrt{2}t\sin\theta-t^2=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}4\sqrt{2}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\cos\theta}\right)\sin\theta-\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\cos\theta}\right)^2&=3\\4\tan\theta-\frac12\sec^2\theta&=3\\8\tan\theta-(1+\tan^2\theta)&=6\\\tan^2\theta-8\tan\theta+7&=0.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence find, to the nearest minute where necessary, the two possible values of $\theta$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}(\tan\theta-1)(\tan\theta-7)&=0\\\tan\theta&=1\text{ or }7\\\theta&=45^\circ\text{ or }\tan^{-1}(7)\\\theta&=45^\circ\text{ or }81^\circ52'\quad\text{(nearest minute).}\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt: A particle is projected from the origin at $50\text{ m/s}$ and passes through $(100,25)$. Let $\theta$ be the angle of projection above the horizontal. Use $g=10\text{ m/s}^2$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the displacement vector by integration.

answer.worked:
The acceleration is
$$\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-10\end{pmatrix}.$$
Integrating,
$$\underset{\sim}{v}=\begin{pmatrix}C_1\\-10t+C_2\end{pmatrix}.$$
At $t=0$, $\underset{\sim}{v}=\begin{pmatrix}50\cos\theta\\50\sin\theta\end{pmatrix}$, so
$$\underset{\sim}{v}=\begin{pmatrix}50\cos\theta\\-10t+50\sin\theta\end{pmatrix}.$$
Integrating again,
$$\underset{\sim}{r}=\begin{pmatrix}50\cos\theta\,t+D_1\\-5t^2+50\sin\theta\,t+D_2\end{pmatrix}.$$
Since the particle starts at the origin, $D_1=D_2=0$. Thus
$$\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}50\cos\theta\,t\\-5t^2+50\sin\theta\,t\end{pmatrix}\text{ m}.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
A particle is projected from the origin at $25\text{ m/s}$ and passes through $(50,10)$. Let $\theta$ be the angle of projection above the horizontal. Use $g=10\text{ m/s}^2$.

Show that $2\tan^2\theta-5\tan\theta+3=0$ and find both possible angles. Give non-exact angles to $1$ decimal place.

answer.worked:
The equations of motion are
$$\begin{align*}x&=25\cos\theta\,t\\y&=-5t^2+25\sin\theta\,t.\end{align*}$$
At $(50,10)$, from the horizontal equation,
$$\begin{align*}50&=25\cos\theta\,t\\t&=\frac{2}{\cos\theta}.\end{align*}$$
Substitute into the vertical equation with $y=10$:
$$\begin{align*}10&=-5\left(\frac{2}{\cos\theta}\right)^2+25\sin\theta\left(\frac{2}{\cos\theta}\right)\\10&=-20\sec^2\theta+50\tan\theta\\10&=-20(1+\tan^2\theta)+50\tan\theta\\20\tan^2\theta-50\tan\theta+30&=0\\2\tan^2\theta-5\tan\theta+3&=0\\(2\tan\theta-3)(\tan\theta-1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Hence $\tan\theta=1$ or $\tan\theta=\frac32$, giving
$$\theta=45^\circ\quad\text{or}\quad\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac32\right)\approx56.3^\circ.$$

content.prompt:
A ball is thrown from the top of a $15\text{ m}$ tower.

Taking the origin at the base, it is projected at $20\text{ m/s}$ and lands $40\text{ m}$ from the base.

Find the two possible angles to 1 d.p.

answer.worked:
Let $\theta$ be the angle of projection above the horizontal. With the origin at the base and $g=10\text{ m/s}^2$,

$$\begin{aligned}x&=20\cos\theta\,t\\y&=-5t^2+20\sin\theta\,t+15\end{aligned}$$
At landing, $x=40$ and $y=0$.

$$\begin{aligned}40&=20\cos\theta\,t\\t&=\frac{2}{\cos\theta}\end{aligned}$$
Substitute into the vertical equation:

$$\begin{aligned}0&=-5\left(\frac{2}{\cos\theta}\right)^2+20\sin\theta\left(\frac{2}{\cos\theta}\right)+15\\0&=-20\sec^2\theta+40\tan\theta+15\\0&=-20(1+\tan^2\theta)+40\tan\theta+15\\20\tan^2\theta-40\tan\theta+5&=0\\4\tan^2\theta-8\tan\theta+1&=0\\\tan\theta&=\frac{8\pm\sqrt{48}}{8}\\\tan\theta&=1\pm\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Hence the two possible angles are

$$\theta\approx61.8^\circ\text{ or }7.6^\circ$$
to 1 d.p., both above the horizontal.

content.prompt: Cooper kicks a football at $12\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and just clears a goalpost 4 m high and 9 m away. Find the two possible angles of projection to the nearest degree.

answer.worked:
Using $g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}$,
$$\begin{aligned}x&=12t\cos\theta\\y&=12t\sin\theta-5t^2.\end{aligned}$$
Substitute $(x,y)=(9,4)$:
$$\begin{aligned}9&=12t\cos\theta\qquad(1)\\4&=12t\sin\theta-5t^2\qquad(2).\end{aligned}$$
From (1),
$$t=\frac{3}{4\cos\theta}.$$
Substitute into (2):
$$\begin{aligned}12\sin\theta\left(\frac{3}{4\cos\theta}\right)-5\left(\frac{3}{4\cos\theta}\right)^2&=4\\9\tan\theta-\frac{45}{16\cos^2\theta}&=4.\end{aligned}$$
Using $\sec^2\theta=1+\tan^2\theta$,
$$\begin{aligned}9\tan\theta-\frac{45}{16}(1+\tan^2\theta)&=4\\45\tan^2\theta-144\tan\theta+109&=0\\\tan\theta&=\frac{144\pm\sqrt{144^2-4(45)(109)}}{90}\\\tan\theta&=\frac{144\pm6\sqrt{31}}{90}\\\theta&\approx51^\circ\text{ or }63^\circ\quad\text{(nearest degree).}\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt: Find the initial speed of the projectile in each case. Give your answers to 1 d.p. Use $g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: A ball is thrown at $45^\circ$ above the horizontal from the top of a $20\text{ m}$ cliff and lands $20\text{ m}$ from the base of the cliff.

answer.worked:
Let $V$ be the initial speed. Take the point of projection as the origin, so the ground is at $y=-20$.
$$\begin{align*}x&=V\cos45^\circ\,t\\y&=V\sin45^\circ\,t-5t^2\end{align*}$$
At landing, $x=20$ and $y=-20$.
$$\begin{align*}20&=V\cos45^\circ\,t\\t&=\frac{20\sqrt2}{V}\end{align*}$$
Substitute into the vertical equation:
$$\begin{align*}-20&=V\sin45^\circ\left(\frac{20\sqrt2}{V}\right)-5\left(\frac{20\sqrt2}{V}\right)^2\\-20&=20-\frac{4000}{V^2}\\\frac{4000}{V^2}&=40\\V^2&=100\\V&=10.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: A ball is thrown from level ground at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal and passes through a point $30\text{ m}$ away horizontally and $5\text{ m}$ above the ground.

answer.worked:
Let $V$ be the initial speed. Take the point of projection as the origin.
$$\begin{align*}x&=V\cos30^\circ\,t\\y&=V\sin30^\circ\,t-5t^2\end{align*}$$
At the point, $x=30$ and $y=5$.
$$\begin{align*}30&=V\cos30^\circ\,t\\t&=\frac{20\sqrt3}{V}\end{align*}$$
Substitute into the vertical equation:
$$\begin{align*}5&=V\sin30^\circ\left(\frac{20\sqrt3}{V}\right)-5\left(\frac{20\sqrt3}{V}\right)^2\\5&=10\sqrt3-\frac{6000}{V^2}\\\frac{6000}{V^2}&=10\sqrt3-5\\V^2&=\frac{6000}{10\sqrt3-5}\\&\approx487.0\\V&\approx22.1\text{ m s}^{-1}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A projectile was fired from level ground and just cleared a wall $10\text{ m}$ high and $20\text{ m}$ from the point of projection. If the angle of projection was $36^\circ$, find the initial speed to the nearest integer.

Note: the height of the wall is not necessarily the maximum height.

answer.worked:
Let $V$ be the initial speed. Take the point of projection as the origin and use $g=10\text{ m/s}^2$.

$$\begin{aligned}x&=V\cos36^\circ\,t\\y&=V\sin36^\circ\,t-5t^2\end{aligned}$$
At the wall, $x=20$ and $y=10$.

$$\begin{aligned}20&=V\cos36^\circ\,t\\t&=\frac{20}{V\cos36^\circ}\end{aligned}$$
Substitute into the vertical equation:

$$\begin{aligned}10&=V\sin36^\circ\left(\frac{20}{V\cos36^\circ}\right)-5\left(\frac{20}{V\cos36^\circ}\right)^2\\10&=20\tan36^\circ-\frac{5(400)}{V^2\cos^236^\circ}\\\frac{5(400)}{V^2\cos^236^\circ}&=20\tan36^\circ-10\\V^2&=\frac{2000}{\cos^236^\circ(20\tan36^\circ-10)}\\V^2&\approx674.5\\V&\approx26\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$
The initial speed is $26\text{ m/s}$ to the nearest integer.

content.prompt: A particle is projected with initial speed $50\text{ m/s}$. On its flight it passes through a point $P$ at horizontal distance $100\text{ m}$ and vertical distance $25\text{ m}$ from the point of projection.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the angle of projection $\alpha$ is $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)$ or $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac92\right)$.

answer.worked:
Using $g=10\text{ m/s}^2$, the equations of motion are
$$\begin{aligned}x&=50\cos\alpha\,t,\\y&=50\sin\alpha\,t-5t^2.\end{aligned}$$
At $P$, $x=100$:
$$\begin{aligned}50\cos\alpha\,t&=100,\\t&=\frac{2}{\cos\alpha}.\end{aligned}$$
Substitute into the vertical equation with $y=25$:
$$\begin{aligned}50\sin\alpha\left(\frac{2}{\cos\alpha}\right)-5\left(\frac{4}{\cos^2\alpha}\right)&=25,\\100\tan\alpha-20\sec^2\alpha&=25,\\100\tan\alpha-20(1+\tan^2\alpha)&=25,\\20\tan^2\alpha-100\tan\alpha+45&=0,\\4\tan^2\alpha-20\tan\alpha+9&=0,\\(2\tan\alpha-1)(2\tan\alpha-9)&=0.\end{aligned}$$
Hence $\tan\alpha=\frac12$ or $\tan\alpha=\frac92$, giving
$$\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)\quad\text{or}\quad\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac92\right).$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: For each angle, find:

children.label: i
children.prompt: the time to reach $P$ (give exact values and approximations to 1 d.p.),

answer.short: For $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)$: $t=\sqrt5\text{ s}\approx2.2\text{ s}$. For $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac92\right)$: $t=\sqrt{85}\text{ s}\approx9.2\text{ s}$.
answer.worked:
For $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)$, $\cos\alpha=\frac{2}{\sqrt5}$:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=\frac{2}{\cos\alpha}\\&=\frac{2}{2/\sqrt5}\\&=\sqrt5\text{ s}\\&\approx2.2\text{ s}.\end{aligned}$$
For $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac92\right)$, $\cos\alpha=\frac{2}{\sqrt{85}}$:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=\frac{2}{\cos\alpha}\\&=\frac{2}{2/\sqrt{85}}\\&=\sqrt{85}\text{ s}\\&\approx9.2\text{ s}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: the velocity at $P$ (to 1 d.p. where necessary).

answer.short: For $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)$: $44.7\text{ m/s}$ horizontally forwards. For $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac92\right)$: $44.7\text{ m/s}$ at $76.0^\circ$ below the horizontal.
answer.worked:
The velocity components are $\dot{x}=50\cos\alpha$ and $\dot{y}=50\sin\alpha-10t$.

For $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)$, $\sin\alpha=\frac1{\sqrt5}$, $\cos\alpha=\frac2{\sqrt5}$ and $t=\sqrt5$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}&=50\cos\alpha\\&=\frac{100}{\sqrt5}\\&=20\sqrt5,\\\dot{y}&=50\sin\alpha-10t\\&=\frac{50}{\sqrt5}-10\sqrt5\\&=10\sqrt5-10\sqrt5\\&=0.\end{aligned}$$
The velocity is $20\sqrt5\text{ m/s}\approx44.7\text{ m/s}$ horizontally forwards. Since $\dot{y}=0$, $P$ is the point of maximum height.

For $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac92\right)$, $\sin\alpha=\frac9{\sqrt{85}}$, $\cos\alpha=\frac2{\sqrt{85}}$ and $t=\sqrt{85}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}&=50\cos\alpha\\&=\frac{100}{\sqrt{85}},\\\dot{y}&=50\sin\alpha-10t\\&=\frac{450}{\sqrt{85}}-10\sqrt{85}\\&=\frac{450-850}{\sqrt{85}}\\&=-\frac{400}{\sqrt{85}}.\end{aligned}$$
Thus
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Speed}&=\sqrt{\dot{x}^{\,2}+\dot{y}^{\,2}}\\&=\sqrt{\frac{100^2+400^2}{85}}\\&=20\sqrt5\text{ m/s}\\&\approx44.7\text{ m/s}.\end{aligned}$$
The horizontal component is positive and the vertical component is negative, so the direction is below the forward horizontal:
$$\begin{aligned}\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{400}{100}\right)\\&=\tan^{-1}(4)\\&\approx76.0^\circ.\end{aligned}$$
The velocity is $44.7\text{ m/s}$ at $76.0^\circ$ below the horizontal.

children.prompt:
A projectile from the origin follows $y=\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{160}x^2$.

Find the angle of projection, the range, and the maximum height.

answer.short:
Angle of projection: $\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac12\right)$.

Range: $80$.

Maximum height: $10$.
answer.worked:
Angle of projection:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx}&=\frac12-\frac{x}{80}\\\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=0}&=\frac12\\\tan\theta&=\frac12\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac12\right).\end{aligned}$$
Range: set $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac12x-\frac{x^2}{160}&=0\\x\left(\frac12-\frac{x}{160}\right)&=0\\x&=0\text{ or }80.\end{aligned}$$
The range is $80$.

Maximum height: set $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac12-\frac{x}{80}&=0\\x&=40\\y(40)&=\frac12(40)-\frac{1}{160}(40)^2\\&=10.\end{aligned}$$
The maximum height is $10$.

children.prompt:

answer.worked:

For the range, set $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-\frac{5x^2}{2304}+\frac{5x}{12}&=0\\\frac{5x}{2304}(192-x)&=0\\x&=0\text{ or }192.\end{aligned}$$
The range is $192\text{ m}$.

$$\begin{aligned}-60&=-35\tan27^\circ-\frac{6125}{V^2\cos^227^\circ}\\\frac{6125}{V^2\cos^227^\circ}&=60-35\tan27^\circ\\V^2&=\frac{6125}{(60-35\tan27^\circ)\cos^227^\circ}\\V&=\sqrt{\frac{6125}{(60-35\tan27^\circ)\cos^227^\circ}}\\V&\approx13.5\text{ m/s}\quad\text{(1 d.p.).}\end{aligned}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: the direction of motion when it lands, to the nearest degree.

answer.worked:
Using the unrounded value of $V$ from part b(i), 

$$\begin{aligned}t&=\frac{35}{V\cos27^\circ}\approx2.90\text{ s},\\\dot{x}&=V\cos27^\circ\approx12.05\text{ m/s},\\\dot{y}&=-10t-V\sin27^\circ\approx-35.17\text{ m/s}.\end{aligned}$$

 If $\phi$ is the angle below the horizontal, 

$$\begin{aligned}\phi&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{|\dot{y}|}{\dot{x}}\right)\\\phi&\approx71^\circ\quad\text{(nearest degree).}\end{aligned}$$

 The direction is $71^\circ$ below the horizontal.

content.prompt:
A gun fires a shell with constant initial speed $V$ and variable angle of elevation $\alpha$.

The displacements after $t$ seconds are $x=Vt\cos\alpha$ and $y=-\frac12gt^2+Vt\sin\alpha$.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Show that the Cartesian equation may be written as
$$gx^2\tan^2\alpha-2xV^2\tan\alpha+(2yV^2+gx^2)=0.$$

answer.worked:
From $x=Vt\cos\alpha$,
$$t=\frac{x}{V\cos\alpha}.$$
Substitute into $y$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=-\frac g2\left(\frac{x}{V\cos\alpha}\right)^2+\frac{Vx\sin\alpha}{V\cos\alpha}\\y&=x\tan\alpha-\frac{gx^2\sec^2\alpha}{2V^2}.\end{aligned}$$
Use $\sec^2\alpha=1+\tan^2\alpha$ and rearrange:
$$\frac{gx^2}{2V^2}(1+\tan^2\alpha)-x\tan\alpha+y=0.$$
Multiply by $2V^2$:
$$gx^2\tan^2\alpha-2xV^2\tan\alpha+(2yV^2+gx^2)=0.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Suppose $V=200\text{ m/s}$ and the shell hits a target $3\text{ km}$ horizontally and $0.5\text{ km}$ vertically from the gun. Take $g=10\text{ m/s}^2$. Show that $\tan\alpha=\frac{4+\sqrt3}{3}$ or $\tan\alpha=\frac{4-\sqrt3}{3}$, and hence find the two possible values of $\alpha$ to the nearest minute.

answer.worked:
Use $V=200$, $x=3000$, $y=500$ and $g=10$, in SI units:
$$\begin{aligned}10(9\times10^6)\tan^2\alpha&-2(3000)(4\times10^4)\tan\alpha\\&+\bigl(2(500)(4\times10^4)+9\times10^7\bigr)=0.\end{aligned}$$
Simplify:
$$\begin{aligned}9\tan^2\alpha-24\tan\alpha+13&=0,\\\tan\alpha&=\frac{24\pm\sqrt{576-468}}{18},\\\tan\alpha&=\frac{24\pm6\sqrt3}{18},\\\tan\alpha&=\frac{4\pm\sqrt3}{3}.\end{aligned}$$
The two angles of elevation are
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4+\sqrt3}{3}\right)\approx62^\circ22',\\\alpha&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4-\sqrt3}{3}\right)\approx37^\circ05'.\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt:
With the Cartesian equation, we can derive the general equation for the range of a projectile.

Using $y=-\dfrac{gx^2}{2V^2}\sec^2\theta+x\tan\theta$, show, using the properties of the sine graph, that the range of an object projected from ground level is $x=\dfrac{V^2}{g}\sin 2\theta$, and explain why the maximum range occurs at an angle of projection of $45^\circ$.

answer.short: $x=\dfrac{V^2}{g}\sin 2\theta$. The maximum range is $\dfrac{V^2}{g}$, attained when $\sin 2\theta=1$, so $\theta=45^\circ$.
answer.worked:
At ground level, $y=0$. For the landing point, $x\ne0$.

$$\begin{align*}x\tan\theta&=\frac{gx^2}{2V^2}\sec^2\theta\\x&=\frac{2V^2\tan\theta}{g\sec^2\theta}\\x&=\frac{2V^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}\\x&=\frac{V^2\sin 2\theta}{g}.\end{align*}$$

The sine graph has $-1\le\sin 2\theta\le1$, so the maximum range is $\dfrac{V^2}{g}$. It occurs when

$$\begin{align*}\sin 2\theta&=1\\2\theta&=90^\circ\\\theta&=45^\circ.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A particle is projected from the origin with initial velocity $60$ m/s at an angle $30^\circ$ to the horizontal.
The acceleration vector is given by
$$\ddot{\mathbf{r}}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-10\end{pmatrix},\quad \text{where }\mathbf{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}x(t)\\y(t)\end{pmatrix}$$
is the position vector.
What are the initial conditions?

(A) $\dot{x}=30\sqrt{3},\ \ddot{x}=-10,\ \dot{y}=30\ \text{ and }\ \ddot{y}=0$
(B) $\dot{x}=30,\ \ddot{x}=-10,\ \dot{y}=30\sqrt{3}\ \text{ and }\ \ddot{y}=0$
(C) $\dot{x}=30,\ \ddot{x}=0,\ \dot{y}=30\sqrt{3}\ \text{ and }\ \ddot{y}=-10$
(D) $\dot{x}=30\sqrt{3},\ \ddot{x}=0,\ \dot{y}=30\ \text{ and }\ \ddot{y}=-10$

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\dot x(0)&=60\cos30^\circ=30\sqrt3\\\dot y(0)&=60\sin30^\circ=30\end{align*}$$From $\ddot{\mathbf r}$, $\ddot x=0$ and $\ddot y=-10$. The answer is (D).

content.prompt:
A projectile has an initial velocity vector $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix}2\sqrt{3}\\2\end{pmatrix}$.
Which of the following is the correct statement of its initial speed and angle of projection from the horizontal?

(A) $4\text{ m/s}$ at $30^\circ$
(B) $\sqrt{10}\text{ m/s}$ at $30^\circ$
(C) $4\text{ m/s}$ at $60^\circ$
(D) $\sqrt{10}\text{ m/s}$ at $60^\circ$

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}|\mathbf v|&=\sqrt{(2\sqrt3)^2+2^2}=4\\\tan\theta&=\frac{2}{2\sqrt3}=\frac1{\sqrt3}\\\theta&=30^\circ\end{align*}$$The answer is (A).

content.prompt:
A projectile is launched from the origin at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal and an initial speed of $U\mathrm{ m s}^{-1}$.
The projectile is $90$ m horizontally from the origin exactly $3$ seconds later.
The acceleration vector due to gravity is $\mathbf{a}=-10\mathbf{j}\mathrm{ m s}^{-2}$.
Calculate the exact initial launch speed $U$ of the projectile.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\dot x&=U\cos30^\circ=\frac{U\sqrt3}{2}\\x&=\frac{U\sqrt3}{2}t\end{align*}$$At $t=3$, $x=90$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{3U\sqrt3}{2}&=90\\U&=\frac{60}{\sqrt3}\\&=20\sqrt3\text{ m s}^{-1}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A particle moves in two dimensional space where $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are unit vectors in the $x$ and $y$ directions respectively.
At time $t$ seconds its displacement from the origin is given by $\mathbf{r}=(6t-4t^2)\mathbf{i}+2t\mathbf{j}$ where all lengths are measured in metres.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Write down the particle's velocity vector in component form.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\mathbf{v}&=\frac{d\mathbf{r}}{dt}\\&=(6-8t)\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}\end{align*}$$In component form this is $\begin{pmatrix}6-8t\\2\end{pmatrix}$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Find the speed of the particle when $t=2$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\mathbf{v}(2)&=-10\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}\\|\mathbf{v}(2)|&=\sqrt{(-10)^2+2^2}\\&=\sqrt{104}\\&=2\sqrt{26}\text{ m/s}\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Show that the equation of the path of the particle is $x=3y-y^2$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}x&=6t-4t^2,\quad y=2t\\t&=\frac{y}{2}\\x&=6\left(\frac y2\right)-4\left(\frac y2\right)^2\\&=3y-y^2\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A particle is projected horizontally with initial speed $50\text{ m s}^{-1}$ from the top of a tower $90$ metres above the origin, as shown in the diagram.
The particle strikes the ground $d$ metres from the base of the tower.

children.label: i
children.prompt:
The acceleration vector due to gravity is $\mathbf{a}=-10\mathbf{j}\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Determine the position vector of the particle, $\mathbf{r}(t)$, where $t$ is the time after projection.

answer.worked:
Integrate the acceleration, using the initial velocity and position to find each constant.
$$\begin{align*}\mathbf{a}&=-10\mathbf{j}\\\mathbf{v}&=-10t\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{C}\end{align*}$$
Since $\mathbf{v}(0)=50\mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{C}=50\mathbf{i}$, so
$$\begin{align*}\mathbf{v}&=50\mathbf{i}-10t\mathbf{j}\\\mathbf{r}&=50t\mathbf{i}-5t^2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{D}\end{align*}$$
Since $\mathbf{r}(0)=90\mathbf{j}$, $\mathbf{D}=90\mathbf{j}$. Therefore
$$\mathbf{r}(t)=\left(50t\,\mathbf{i}+(90-5t^2)\mathbf{j}\right)\text{ m}.$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Find the exact time taken for the particle to strike the ground.

answer.worked:
At ground level the vertical component of position is zero.
$$\begin{align*}90-5t^2&=0\\t^2&=18\\t&=\sqrt{18}\quad(t>0)\\&=3\sqrt{2}\text{ s}\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt:
Find the speed of the particle when it strikes the ground.
Give your answer correct to one decimal place.

answer.worked:
At $t=\sqrt{18}$,
$$\begin{align*}\mathbf{v}&=50\mathbf{i}-10\sqrt{18}\,\mathbf{j}\\\lvert\mathbf{v}\rvert&=\sqrt{50^2+(10\sqrt{18})^2}\\&=\sqrt{2500+1800}\\&=65.574\ldots\\&\approx65.6\text{ m s}^{-1}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A rocket is fired with a velocity $V\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal from sea level and hits a cliff face as shown.
Neglect air resistance and take $g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}$.

children.label: i
children.prompt:
If $V=180\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $\theta=60^\circ$, show that at any time $t$ seconds, the position vector of the rocket relative to the point at which it was fired is
$$\mathbf{s}(t)=90t\mathbf{i}+(90\sqrt{3}t-5t^2)\mathbf{j}.$$

answer.worked:
The initial velocity components are
$$\begin{align*}\dot{x}_0&=180\cos60^\circ=90,\\\dot{y}_0&=180\sin60^\circ=90\sqrt{3}.\end{align*}$$
Horizontally:
$$\begin{align*}\ddot{x}&=0\\\dot{x}&=90\\x&=90t.\end{align*}$$
Vertically:
$$\begin{align*}\ddot{y}&=-10\\\dot{y}&=-10t+90\sqrt{3}\\y&=-5t^2+90\sqrt{3}t.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\mathbf{s}(t)=90t\mathbf{i}+(90\sqrt{3}t-5t^2)\mathbf{j}$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Find the maximum height reached by the rocket.

answer.worked:
The maximum height occurs when $\dot{y}=0$.
$$\begin{align*}-10t+90\sqrt{3}&=0\\t&=9\sqrt{3}.\end{align*}$$
Substitute into $y=-5t^2+90\sqrt{3}t$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=-5(9\sqrt{3})^2+90\sqrt{3}(9\sqrt{3})\\&=-1215+2430\\&=1215\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt:
The base of the cliff is $270\,\text{m}$ from the point at which the rocket was fired.
Find the value of $h$.

answer.worked:
The cliff is reached when $x=270$.
$$\begin{align*}270&=90t\\t&=3.\end{align*}$$
Then:
$$\begin{align*}h&=-5(3)^2+90\sqrt{3}(3)\\&=270\sqrt{3}-45\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A cannonball is fired from a cannon sitting on the top of a cliff into the sea.
Initially, the cannonball is $50$ metres above the foot of the cliff and its velocity vector at that time is $30\sqrt{3}\mathbf{i} + 15\mathbf{j}$, measured in metres per second.
The acceleration due to gravity is a constant $9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ for the duration of the cannonball's flight and air resistance is negligible.
Use the foot of the cliff as the origin as shown in the diagram above.
You are also given that the velocity vector of the cannonball $t$ seconds after it was fired is:
$\mathbf{v}(t) = 30\sqrt{3}\mathbf{i} + (15 - 9.8t)\mathbf{j}$.
Do NOT prove this.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Calculate the initial speed of the cannonball correct to the nearest metre per second.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Initial speed}&=\sqrt{(30\sqrt{3})^2+15^2}\\&=\sqrt{2925}\\&\approx54\text{ m/s}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Find the size of the angle at which the cannonball was fired correct to the nearest degree.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{15}{30\sqrt{3}}\right)\\&\approx16^\circ.\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Write down the position vector, $\mathbf{r}(t)$, of the cannonball.

answer.worked:
$$\mathbf{r}(t)=30\sqrt{3}t\mathbf{i}+(15t-4.9t^2)\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{c}.$$
Since $\mathbf{r}(0)=50\mathbf{j}$, $\mathbf{c}=50\mathbf{j}$.
$$\mathbf{r}(t)=30\sqrt{3}t\mathbf{i}+(50+15t-4.9t^2)\mathbf{j}.$$

children.label: iv
children.prompt:
Determine the greatest height above sea level achieved by the cannonball.
Express your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

answer.worked:
The greatest height occurs when $\dot{y}=0$.
$$\begin{align*}15-9.8t&=0\\t&=\frac{15}{9.8}.\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}y&=50+15\left(\frac{15}{9.8}\right)-4.9\left(\frac{15}{9.8}\right)^2\\&\approx61.48\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: v
children.prompt:
How long will it take for the cannonball to land on the surface of the sea?
Express your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

answer.worked:
The cannonball lands when $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}50+15t-4.9t^2&=0\\t&=\frac{-15-\sqrt{15^2-4(-4.9)(50)}}{2(-4.9)}\\&\approx5.07\text{ s}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A particle is projected with an initial velocity $V\text{ m/s}$ at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, from a point $O$ on the edge of a vertical cliff $32$ metres above a horizontal beach.
This particle moves in a vertical plane under gravity, and its position vector, $\mathbf{r}(t)$, is given by:
$$\mathbf{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}Vt\cos\theta \\ Vt\sin\theta-5t^2\end{pmatrix}$$
Do NOT prove this.
The particle hits the beach after $4$ seconds, $64$ metres from the foot of the cliff.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Find the exact value of $V$ and find the value of $\theta$, to the nearest degree.

answer.worked:
At $t=4$, $x=64$ and $y=-32$.
$$\begin{align*}64&=4V\cos\theta\\V\cos\theta&=16\\-32&=4V\sin\theta-80\\V\sin\theta&=12\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}V^2&=16^2+12^2\\&=400\\V&=20\text{ m/s}\\\tan\theta&=\frac{12}{16}\\&=\frac{3}{4}\\\theta&\approx37^\circ.\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Find the speed of impact with the beach correct to the nearest $\text{m/s}$ and the angle of impact with the beach correct to the nearest degree.

answer.short: Speed $\approx32\text{ m/s}$, angle $\approx60^\circ$ to the horizontal
answer.worked:
With $V=20$, $\sin\theta=\frac35$ and $\cos\theta=\frac45$:
$$\begin{align*}\mathbf{r}(t)&=16t\,\mathbf{i}+(12t-5t^2)\,\mathbf{j}\\\mathbf{v}(t)&=16\,\mathbf{i}+(12-10t)\,\mathbf{j}\\\mathbf{v}(4)&=16\,\mathbf{i}-28\,\mathbf{j}\\|\mathbf{v}(4)|&=\sqrt{16^2+(-28)^2}\\&=\sqrt{1040}\\&\approx32\text{ m/s}\\\tan\alpha&=\frac{28}{16}\\\alpha&\approx60^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The particle hits the beach at about $32\text{ m/s}$ at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal.

Initially, the velocity vector of the ball is $(5\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j})$ m/s, where $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are the unit vectors in the horizontal and vertical directions respectively.
After being struck, the ball undergoes projectile motion under the influence of gravity only, that is, the acceleration vector of the ball is $\mathbf{a} = -10\mathbf{j}$.
The ball will hit the ground at point $B$, a point that is on the same horizontal level as the origin.

spec.description: Axes with origin O, point A on the vertical axis, a parabolic path leaving A with initial velocity arrow labelled 5i+8j and landing at B on the horizontal axis.
spec.mathematics: Path r = 5t i + (21+8t-5t^2) j for 0<=t<=3; B at x=15. Drawing coordinates are scaled and schematic.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied question diagram; no calculated values shown.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the velocity vector of the ball $t$ seconds after being struck is $\mathbf{v} = 5\mathbf{i} + (8 - 10t)\mathbf{j}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{v}&=\int(-10\mathbf{j})\,dt\\\mathbf{v}&=c_1\mathbf{i}+(-10t+c_2)\mathbf{j}\\\mathbf{v}(0)&=5\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j}\\c_1&=5,\quad c_2=8\\\mathbf{v}&=5\mathbf{i}+(8-10t)\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find an expression for the position vector $\mathbf{r}$ of the ball relative to $O$ at a time $t$ seconds after it was struck.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}&=\int\left(5\mathbf{i}+(8-10t)\mathbf{j}\right)dt\\\mathbf{r}&=5t\mathbf{i}+(8t-5t^2+C)\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}$$
(the horizontal constant is $0$ since the horizontal component of $\mathbf{r}(0)$ is $0$). Using $\mathbf{r}(0)=21\mathbf{j}$ gives $C=21$.
$$\mathbf{r}=5t\mathbf{i}+(21+8t-5t^2)\mathbf{j}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the maximum height that the ball reaches.

answer.worked:
At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero.
$$\begin{aligned}8-10t&=0\\t&=0.8\\y&=21+8(0.8)-5(0.8)^2\\&=21+6.4-3.2\\&=24.2\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the speed of the ball when it lands at $B$ and the angle at which the ball strikes the ground.

answer.short: Speed $\sqrt{509}\approx22.56$ m/s, at approximately $77^\circ$ below the horizontal.
answer.worked:
The ball lands when $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}21+8t-5t^2&=0\\5t^2-8t-21&=0\\(5t+7)(t-3)&=0\\t&=3\quad(t\geq0)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{v}(3)&=5\mathbf{i}+(8-30)\mathbf{j}\\&=5\mathbf{i}-22\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}|\mathbf{v}(3)|&=\sqrt{5^2+(-22)^2}\\&=\sqrt{509}\\&\approx22.56\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{22}{5}\right)\\&\approx77^\circ\end{aligned}$$
The vertical component is negative, so the angle is below the horizontal.

classification.difficultyReason: The given acceleration and initial vector lead through scaffolded integration, initial conditions, maximum height and impact. The hardest essential demand links landing time to the velocity components and interprets their magnitude and direction; these are routine taught procedures.

content.prompt:
Jerry stands at the top of a building $30 \text{ m}$ tall and throws a ball with a velocity of $15 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $45^\circ$ to the horizontal.
The ball eventually reaches the ground.

children.label: i
children.prompt:
Derive the vector displacement of the ball in the form $\mathbf{s}=x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j}$.
You may assume that $g=10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.

answer.worked:
Take the launch point as $(0,30)$, so $x(0)=0$ and $y(0)=30$.
$$\begin{align*}\ddot{x}&=0, & \ddot{y}&=-10\\\dot{x}&=15\cos45^\circ=\frac{15\sqrt2}{2}, & \dot{y}&=-10t+15\sin45^\circ=-10t+\frac{15\sqrt2}{2}\\x&=\frac{15\sqrt2}{2}t, & y&=-5t^2+\frac{15\sqrt2}{2}t+30\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Find the time taken for the ball to reach the ground.

answer.worked:
Let $y=0$:
$$\begin{align*}-5t^2+\frac{15\sqrt2}{2}t+30&=0\\t&=\frac{\frac{15\sqrt2}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{225}{2}+600}}{10}\\&\approx3.7\text{ s}\end{align*}$$Reject the negative root.

classification.difficultyReason: Resolve the initial velocity, derive both displacement components, and solve a quadratic for the positive landing time.

content.prompt:
The position vector of a projectile, fired from the origin with velocity $V \text{ m/s}$, after $t$ seconds is given by
$$\mathbf{r}(t) = \frac{V}{2}t\mathbf{i} + \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}V}{2}t - 5t^2\right)\mathbf{j}.$$
Find the minimum velocity required for the projectile to reach a height of $40$ metres.
Round your answer to the nearest $\text{m/s}$.

answer.worked:
At maximum height, $\dot y=0$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{\sqrt3V}{2}-10t&=0\\t&=\frac{\sqrt3V}{20}\end{align*}$$Maximum height:
$$\begin{align*}y&=\frac{\sqrt3V}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3V}{20}-5\cdot\frac{3V^2}{400}\\&=\frac{3V^2}{80}\end{align*}$$Let $y=40$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{3V^2}{80}&=40\\V^2&=\frac{3200}{3}\\V&\approx33\text{ m/s}\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that the minimum launch speed occurs when the maximum height is exactly 40 m, then solve for the speed.

content.prompt:
A particle, $A$, is projected from the origin with an initial velocity of $16\mathbf{i}+30\mathbf{j}\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
At the same time, particle $B$ is projected from a point that is $60\text{ m}$ to the right of the origin and $25\text{ m}$ above the origin with an initial velocity of $-8\mathbf{i}+20\mathbf{j}\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Let the acceleration due to gravity be $9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
The position vector of particle $A$ at time $t$ seconds is given by $16t\mathbf{i}+(30t-4.9t^2)\mathbf{j}$.
(Do NOT prove this.)

children.label: i
children.prompt: Find the position vector of particle $B$ at time $t$ seconds.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\ddot x&=0,\ \dot x=-8,\ x=60-8t\\\ddot y&=-9.8,\ \dot y=20-9.8t,\ y=25+20t-4.9t^2\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Find the time and point at which the two particles collide.

answer.worked:
Equate horizontal components:
$$\begin{align*}16t&=60-8t\\t&=2.5\end{align*}$$Then
$$\begin{align*}x&=16(2.5)=40\\y&=30(2.5)-4.9(2.5)^2=44.375\end{align*}$$(Check with $B$: $25+50-30.625=44.375$.)

classification.difficultyReason: Form the second position vector and check that both particles have the same horizontal and vertical positions at the same time.

content.prompt:
A projectile is launched from the origin with an initial speed of $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $\alpha$ to the horizontal.
Assume that $g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

children.label: i
children.prompt: If the projectile must land on a target that is located 20 m from the origin on the horizontal, at what angles should it be launched?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}x&=20t\cos\alpha, & y&=20t\sin\alpha-5t^2\end{align*}$$Landing: $y=0$ gives $t=4\sin\alpha$.
$$\begin{align*}20&=20(4\sin\alpha)\cos\alpha\\20&=40\sin2\alpha\\\sin2\alpha&=\frac12\\2\alpha&=\frac\pi6,\ \frac{5\pi}6\\\alpha&=\frac\pi{12},\ \frac{5\pi}{12}\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt:
Find the time of flight for each of the angles from part (i).
Give your answers correct to two decimal places.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}t&=4\sin\frac\pi{12}\approx1.04\text{ s}\\t&=4\sin\frac{5\pi}{12}\approx3.86\text{ s}\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Use the landing condition and horizontal range to solve a trigonometric equation for two launch angles, then find both flight times.

content.prompt:
In this question take upwards as positive, $g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and ignore air resistance.
A tennis ball is hit from a point $2$ metres above a level court.
The vertical component of the velocity of the ball immediately after being hit is $12\text{ m s}^{-1}$ upwards.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Write an expression for $\dot{y}$, the vertical component of the ball's velocity $t$ seconds after being hit.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\dot y&=-10t+C\\\dot y(0)&=12\Rightarrow C=12\\\dot y&=-10t+12\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence find how long it takes for the ball to reach its maximum height above the court.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}0&=-10t+12\\t&=\frac65\text{ s}\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Write an expression for $y$, the vertical displacement of the ball above the court $t$ seconds after being hit.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}y&=-5t^2+12t+C\\y(0)&=2\Rightarrow C=2\\y&=-5t^2+12t+2\end{align*}$$

children.label: iv
children.prompt:
Find how much time passes between the ball being hit and the ball falling to the court.
Give your answer as an exact value in seconds.

answer.worked:
Let $y=0$:
$$\begin{align*}5t^2-12t-2&=0\\t&=\frac{12\pm\sqrt{184}}{10}\\&=\frac{6\pm\sqrt{46}}{5}\end{align*}$$Since $t>0$, $t=\frac{6+\sqrt{46}}{5}$ s.

children.label: v
children.prompt:
The ball initially leaves the racket at an angle of $60^\circ$ to the horizontal.
Calculate the horizontal distance travelled by the ball during its flight.
Give your answer in metres, correct to the nearest centimetre.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}V\sin60^\circ&=12\Rightarrow V=8\sqrt3\\\dot x&=8\sqrt3\cos60^\circ=4\sqrt3\\x&=4\sqrt3\cdot\frac{6+\sqrt{46}}{5}\\&\approx17.71\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Find the positive root for the flight time, infer horizontal velocity from the vertical component and launch angle, and combine them for distance.

content.prompt:
When an object is projected from a point $h$ metres above the origin with initial speed $V \text{ m/s}$ at an angle of $\theta^\circ$ to the horizontal, its displacement vector, $t$ seconds after projection, is
$$\vec{r}(t) = (Vt \cos \theta)\mathbf{i} + (-5t^2 + Vt \sin \theta + h)\mathbf{j}$$
(Do NOT prove this.)
A person, standing in an empty room which is $3 \text{ m}$ high, throws a ball at the far wall of the room.
The ball leaves their hand $1 \text{ m}$ above the floor and $10 \text{ m}$ from the far wall.
The initial velocity of the ball is $12 \text{ m/s}$ at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal.
Show that the ball will NOT hit the ceiling of the room but that it will hit the far wall without hitting the floor.

answer.short: The maximum height is $2.8\text{ m} < 3\text{ m}$, so the ball misses the ceiling. At the far wall ($x=10$) the height is $y=\frac{10\sqrt3}{3}-\frac{98}{27}\approx 2.14\text{ m}$, which is above the floor, so the ball hits the wall without hitting the floor.
answer.worked:
Take the origin on the floor directly below the launch point, so $V=12$, $\theta=30^\circ$, $h=1$. The floor is $y=0$, the ceiling is $y=3$ and the far wall is $x=10$.
$$\begin{aligned}x(t)&=12t\cos30^\circ=6\sqrt3\,t\\y(t)&=-5t^2+12t\sin30^\circ+1=-5t^2+6t+1\end{aligned}$$
**Ceiling.** The ball is at maximum height when $\dot y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dot y&=-10t+6=0\\t&=0.6\text{ s}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y_{\max}&=-5(0.6)^2+6(0.6)+1\\&=-1.8+3.6+1\\&=2.8\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
Since $2.8<3$, the ball does NOT hit the ceiling.

**Far wall.** The ball reaches the wall when $x=10$.
$$\begin{aligned}6\sqrt3\,t&=10\\t&=\frac{5}{3\sqrt3}\approx0.96\text{ s}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y&=-5\left(\frac{25}{27}\right)+6\left(\frac{5}{3\sqrt3}\right)+1\\&=-\frac{125}{27}+\frac{10\sqrt3}{3}+1\\&=\frac{10\sqrt3}{3}-\frac{98}{27}\\&\approx5.7735-3.6296\\&\approx2.14\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
Since $0<2.14<3$, the ball is above the floor and below the ceiling when it reaches the wall. The ball rises to $2.8\text{ m}$ and then falls, so its height stays above $1\text{ m}$ until the time it reaches $x=10$, where it is $2.14\text{ m}$ above the floor. Hence the ball hits the far wall without hitting the floor.

classification.difficultyReason: The student must translate the room constraints into a maximum-height comparison and a height check at the wall, linking the horizontal and vertical equations through time and interpreting the trajectory between launch and impact.

content.prompt:
A golfer hits a golf ball from a point $O$ with speed $V$ m/s at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal, where $0^\circ<\theta<90^\circ$.
The ball just passes over a $2.25$ m high tree after $1.5$ seconds.
The tree is $60$ metres away on level ground from the point from which the ball was hit.
The acceleration due to gravity is $10\text{ m/s}^2$.
The position vector, $\mathbf{r}$, at any time, $t$ seconds, is given by
$$\mathbf{r}(t)=Vt\cos\theta\,\mathbf{i}+\left(Vt\sin\theta-5t^2\right)\mathbf{j}.$$
Do not prove this.

children.label: i
children.prompt: What is the initial angle, $\theta$, of projection of the golf ball, to the nearest minute?

answer.worked:
At $t=1.5$ the ball is at $(60,2.25)$.
$$\begin{align*}1.5V\cos\theta&=60\Rightarrow V\cos\theta=40\\1.5V\sin\theta-11.25&=2.25\Rightarrow V\sin\theta=9\end{align*}$$$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac9{40}\\\theta&\approx12^\circ41'\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: What is the initial speed $(V\text{ m/s})$ of the golf ball?

children.label: iii
children.prompt:
How far from the base of the tree does the ball strike the ground?
Leave your answer correct to the nearest metre.

answer.worked:
$y=9t-5t^2=0$ gives $t=\frac95$.
$$x=40\times\frac95=72\text{ m}$$Distance from the tree: $72-60=12$ m.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover the initial velocity components from the known position and time, then find the angle, speed, and landing distance relative to the tree.

content.prompt:
A ball is projected upwards from the origin on a horizontal surface with an initial velocity of $\mathbf{v}(0) = \begin{pmatrix} 20 \\ 20\sqrt{3} \end{pmatrix} \text{ m/s}$.
Assume $\mathbf{a}(t) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -g \end{pmatrix}$, where $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, and that air resistance is negligible.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Prove that the velocity $t$ seconds after projection is given by $\mathbf{v}(t) = \begin{pmatrix} 20 \\ 20\sqrt{3} - 10t \end{pmatrix}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\mathbf{v}(t)&=\begin{pmatrix}C_1\\-10t+C_2\end{pmatrix}\\\mathbf{v}(0)&=\begin{pmatrix}20\\20\sqrt3\end{pmatrix}\Rightarrow C_1=20,\ C_2=20\sqrt3\\\therefore\ \mathbf{v}(t)&=\begin{pmatrix}20\\20\sqrt3-10t\end{pmatrix}\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Find how long the ball is in the air before impact with the horizontal surface.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}y&=-5t^2+20\sqrt3\,t\\0&=5t(-t+4\sqrt3)\\t&=4\sqrt3\text{ s}\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Prove that the maximum magnitude of $\mathbf{v}(t)$ at any time during flight is twice its minimum magnitude.

answer.worked:
$|\mathbf v|^2=400+(20\sqrt3-10t)^2$ is smallest when $\dot y=0$ (at $t=2\sqrt3$) and largest at $t=0$ and $t=4\sqrt3$, where $|\dot y|=20\sqrt3$.
$$\begin{align*}|\mathbf v|_{\max}&=\sqrt{20^2+(20\sqrt3)^2}=40\\|\mathbf v|_{\min}&=\sqrt{20^2+0^2}=20\\|\mathbf v|_{\max}&=2|\mathbf v|_{\min}\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Find the flight interval and interpret the extrema of speed using the constant horizontal component and changing vertical component.

content.prompt:
The displacement of a projectile fired from the origin $O$ has a horizontal component $x$ and a vertical component $y$.
The equations of motion are
$$x=Vt\cos\alpha,$$
$$y=Vt\sin\alpha-5t^2,$$
where $V$ is the initial speed in metres per second, $\alpha$ is the angle of projection as in the diagram, and $t$ is the time in seconds.
The range, $R$, is the total horizontal distance travelled by the projectile.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Derive an expression for $R$ in terms of $V$ and $\alpha$.

answer.worked:
At the end of the flight, $y=0$:
$$\begin{align*}Vt\sin\alpha-5t^2&=0\\t(V\sin\alpha-5t)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Ignoring $t=0$, $t=\dfrac{V\sin\alpha}{5}$. Substituting into $x=Vt\cos\alpha$:
$$\begin{align*}R&=V\cos\alpha\cdot\frac{V\sin\alpha}{5}\\&=\frac{V^2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}{5}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt:
The maximum range for a given value of $V$ is $R_{\max}$.
Show that $R_{\max}$ occurs when $\alpha=45^\circ$ and obtain a fully simplified expression for it.

answer.worked:
Using $\sin2\alpha=2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha$:
$$R=\frac{V^2\sin2\alpha}{10}.$$
The maximum of $\sin2\alpha$ is $1$, when $2\alpha=90^\circ$, so $\alpha=45^\circ$. Therefore
$$R_{\max}=\frac{V^2}{10}.$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Show that if the projectile is to hit a target $12\text{ km}$ away, it must be launched at a speed faster than the speed of sound in air, which is $343\text{ m/s}$.

answer.worked:
The maximum range must be at least $12\,000\text{ m}$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{V^2}{10}&\ge12\,000\\V^2&\ge120\,000\\V&\ge346.4\text{ m/s}.\end{align*}$$
Since $346.4>343$, the speed must exceed the speed of sound.

spec.description: A dashed parabolic trajectory from the origin returning to the x-axis. The velocity vector V leaves the origin at angle alpha to the x-axis, and the range R is marked by a double-headed dimension arrow below the x-axis.
spec.mathematics: Trajectory y = 1.1x(1 - x/10) on 0 <= x <= 10, so the range is R = 10 in the plotted units. V is along the tangent at the origin and alpha is the angle between V and the x-axis.
spec.answerVisibility: No numeric values are given. The origin is unlabelled, as the house style requires.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive the range from the nonzero flight time, maximise it using a trigonometric identity, and apply the resulting bound to the target distance.

content.prompt:
A particle is projected from a point $O$ on level horizontal ground with a speed of $21\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal.
At time $T$ seconds, the particle passes through the point $B(12,2)$.
Neglecting the effects of air resistance, the equations describing the motion of the particle are:
$$x=Vt\cos\theta$$
$$y=Vt\sin\theta-\frac{1}{2}gt^2$$
where $t$ is the time in seconds after projection, $g=9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ is the acceleration due to gravity, and $x$ and $y$ are measured in metres.
Do NOT prove these equations.

children.label: i
children.prompt: By considering the horizontal component of the particle's motion, show that $T=\frac{4}{7}\sec\theta$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}12&=21T\cos\theta\\T&=\frac{12}{21\cos\theta}\\&=\frac47\sec\theta\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: By considering the vertical component of the particle's motion and, using the result from part (i), show that $4\tan^2\theta-30\tan\theta+9=0$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}2&=21T\sin\theta-4.9T^2\\&=12\tan\theta-\frac85\sec^2\theta\\&=12\tan\theta-\frac85(1+\tan^2\theta)\\10&=60\tan\theta-8-8\tan^2\theta\\4\tan^2\theta-30\tan\theta+9&=0\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt:
Find the particle's least possible flight time from $O$ to $B$.
Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

answer.worked:
$$\tan\theta=\frac{15\pm3\sqrt{21}}{4}$$The shorter time comes from the smaller $\tan\theta$, $\frac{15-3\sqrt{21}}{4}$.
$$\begin{align*}T&=\frac47\sqrt{1+\tan^2\theta}\\&\approx0.60\text{ s}\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Use the scaffolded component equations to form a quadratic in tan theta, then select the angle giving the shorter travel time.

content.prompt:
A boy throws a ball from point $A$, which is $2$ m above the ground, with initial speed $V\mathrm{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $\theta$ to the horizontal.
The position vector of the ball, $\mathbf{r}$, where $t$ is the time after projection and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, is given by
$$\mathbf{r}=(Vt\cos\theta)\mathbf{i}+\left(Vt\sin\theta-\frac{gt^2}{2}+2\right)\mathbf{j}$$
(Do NOT prove this.)

children.label: i
children.prompt:
The highest point reached by the ball is $3$ m above the ground.
Show that $V^2=\frac{2g}{\sin^2\theta}$.

answer.worked:
Differentiating the position vector gives the velocity vector
$$\mathbf{v}=(V\cos\theta)\mathbf{i}+(V\sin\theta-gt)\mathbf{j}.$$
At maximum height, the vertical component of velocity is zero:
$$\begin{align*}
V\sin\theta-gt &= 0 \\
t &= \frac{V\sin\theta}{g}.
\end{align*}$$
At this time, $y=3$. Using $y=Vt\sin\theta-\frac{gt^2}{2}+2$,
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{g}-\frac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}+2&=3 \\
\frac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g} &= 1 \\
V^2\sin^2\theta &= 2g \\
V^2 &= \frac{2g}{\sin^2\theta}.
\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt:
The point $T$ is at a horizontal distance of $20$ m from $A$ and is at a height of $0.75$ m above ground.
The ball reaches $T$ without hitting the ground.
Show that $\tan\theta=\frac{1}{4}$.

answer.worked:
When the horizontal displacement is $20$ m,
$$\begin{align*}
Vt\cos\theta &= 20 \\
t &= \frac{20}{V\cos\theta}.
\end{align*}$$
At this time, $y=0.75$:
$$\begin{align*}
20\tan\theta-\frac{200g}{V^2\cos^2\theta}+2&=0.75 \\
20\tan\theta-\frac{200g}{V^2\cos^2\theta}+\frac{5}{4}&=0.
\end{align*}$$
Using $V^2=\frac{2g}{\sin^2\theta}$ from part (i),
$$\begin{align*}
20\tan\theta-100\tan^2\theta+\frac{5}{4} &= 0 \\
400\tan^2\theta-80\tan\theta-5 &= 0 \\
\tan\theta &= \frac{80\pm\sqrt{(-80)^2-4(400)(-5)}}{2(400)} \\
&= \frac{1}{4},\ -\frac{1}{20}.
\end{align*}$$
Since $0<\theta<90^\circ$, $\tan\theta>0$, so the negative solution is rejected. Therefore, $\tan\theta=\frac{1}{4}$.

spec.description: Projectile path of a ball from A, 2 m above the ground on the y-axis, rising to a maximum height of 3 m and descending to point T. The initial velocity V is shown as an arrow from A at angle θ above a dashed horizontal line. Vertical dimension arrows show 2 m (ground to A) and 3 m (ground to the highest point).
spec.mathematics: A is 2 m above the ground; maximum height is 3 m above the ground; the launch angle is θ to the horizontal; T is the end of the path. Not to scale: the path is a parabola drawn through A, the apex and T, with the apex placed where the 3 m arrow is drawn.
spec.answerVisibility: T's height (0.75 m), its horizontal distance (20 m), the value of V and tan θ are not shown, as in the source.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the zero vertical velocity at maximum height, then eliminate time and speed to form a quadratic in tan θ and reject the solution inconsistent with the launch direction.

content.prompt:
A student kicks a football from ground level.
The ball is kicked at an angle of projection of $\theta$ at a speed of $V$ metres per second.
The displacement vector of the ball from the student's position, $t$ seconds after it is kicked, is given by
$$\mathbf{r}(t)=(Vt\cos\theta)\mathbf{i}+(Vt\sin\theta-5t^2)\mathbf{j}.$$
Two seconds after being kicked, the ball just clears the far side of a $5$ metre high building.
The building is $5$ metres wide, and the closest wall of the building is $10$ metres from the student.
Let $d_1$ be the distance by which it clears the closest wall of the building, and $d_2$ be the distance from the far wall of the building to the point of impact, as shown.
Show that the difference between $d_2$ and $d_1$ is less than $1$, i.e.
$d_2-d_1<1$.

answer.short: $d_2-d_1=\dfrac{35}{36}<1$. Use the conditions at $t=2$ to find $V\cos\theta$ and $V\sin\theta$, then find $d_1$ and $d_2$.
answer.worked:
Let $x=Vt\cos\theta$ and $y=Vt\sin\theta-5t^2$. At $t=2$, $x=15$ and $y=5$.
$$\begin{align*}15&=2V\cos\theta\\V\cos\theta&=\frac{15}{2}\\5&=2V\sin\theta-20\\V\sin\theta&=\frac{25}{2}\end{align*}$$
At the closest wall, $x=10$:
$$\begin{align*}10&=\frac{15}{2}t\\t&=\frac{4}{3}\\y&=\frac{25}{2}\cdot\frac{4}{3}-5\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^2\\&=\frac{50}{3}-\frac{80}{9}\\&=\frac{70}{9}\\d_1&=\frac{70}{9}-5\\&=\frac{25}{9}\end{align*}$$
At impact, $y=0$:
$$\begin{align*}0&=\frac{25}{2}t-5t^2\\0&=t\left(\frac{25}{2}-5t\right)\\t&=\frac{5}{2}\\x&=\frac{15}{2}\cdot\frac{5}{2}\\&=\frac{75}{4}\\d_2&=\frac{75}{4}-15\\&=\frac{15}{4}\end{align*}$$
Therefore
$$\begin{align*}d_2-d_1&=\frac{15}{4}-\frac{25}{9}\\&=\frac{135-100}{36}\\&=\frac{35}{36}\\&<1.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
In the diagram, points $A$ and $B$ are separated by a horizontal distance $R$ and point $B$ is located $H$ metres higher than $A$.
Define the angle of inclination of $B$ from $A$ as $\alpha$.
Define the origin for both motions at point $A$ and positive directions as right and up respectively.
At the same instant, identical projectiles are launched from each location directed towards each other.
The projectile from $A$ is fired with initial speed $U\text{ m/s}$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal while the object launched from $B$ has only half as much initial speed but the same angle of elevation above the horizontal.
Consequently, the equations of motion for the projectile from $A$, $t$ seconds after launch, are as follows:
$$x_A=Ut\cos\theta$$
$$y_A=Ut\sin\theta-\frac{1}{2}gt^2.$$
Similarly for the projectile from $B$:
$$x_B=R-\frac{Ut\cos\theta}{2}$$
$$y_B=H+\frac{Ut\sin\theta}{2}-\frac{1}{2}gt^2.$$
Do not prove these equations.
Given that the projectiles collide, show that this requires
$$\tan\alpha=\frac{1}{3}\tan\theta.$$

spec.description: Axes x and y with A at the origin and B up and to the right. Dashed line AB at angle alpha to the horizontal, R marked along the horizontal and H marked as the vertical height of B above A. Projectile from A with speed U at angle theta above the horizontal; projectile from B with speed U/2 directed up and to the left at angle theta above the horizontal (measured from the leftward horizontal).
spec.mathematics: tan(alpha)=H/R. The speed and angle labels are the given data; drawing coordinates are schematic.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied question diagram.

answer.short: Equating coordinates gives $t=\dfrac{2R}{3U\cos\theta}=\dfrac{2H}{U\sin\theta}$, so $\dfrac HR=\dfrac13\tan\theta$, i.e. $\tan\alpha=\dfrac13\tan\theta$.
answer.worked:
For the projectiles to collide, their $x$-coordinates must be equal.
$$\begin{aligned}x_A&=x_B\\Ut\cos\theta&=R-\frac{Ut\cos\theta}{2}\\\frac32Ut\cos\theta&=R\\t&=\frac{2R}{3U\cos\theta}\end{aligned}$$
Their $y$-coordinates must also be equal.
$$\begin{aligned}y_A&=y_B\\Ut\sin\theta-\frac12gt^2&=H+\frac{Ut\sin\theta}{2}-\frac12gt^2\\\frac12Ut\sin\theta&=H\\t&=\frac{2H}{U\sin\theta}\end{aligned}$$
Equate the two expressions for $t$.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{2R}{3U\cos\theta}&=\frac{2H}{U\sin\theta}\\R\sin\theta&=3H\cos\theta\\\frac HR&=\frac13\tan\theta\end{aligned}$$
Since $\tan\alpha=\dfrac HR$,
$$\tan\alpha=\frac13\tan\theta.$$

classification.difficultyReason: Both coordinate models and the target relation are supplied, but the student must connect simultaneous equality in two dimensions, cancel gravity and relate the resulting height-to-distance ratio to α. This is a non-trivial connection with substantial scaffolding.

content.prompt:
A golfer hits a golf ball with initial speed $V\text{ ms}^{-1}$ at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal.

The golf ball is hit from one side of a lake and must have a horizontal range of $100\text{ m}$ or more to avoid landing in the lake.

Neglecting the effects of air resistance, the equations describing the motion of the ball are
$$\begin{align*}x&=Vt\cos\theta\\y&=Vt\sin\theta-\frac12gt^2\end{align*}$$
where $t$ is the time in seconds after the ball is hit and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity in $\text{ms}^{-2}$.

Do NOT prove these equations.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Show that the horizontal range of the golf ball is $\dfrac{V^2\sin2\theta}{g}$ metres.

answer.worked:
The range is the value of $x$ when $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}Vt\sin\theta-\frac12gt^2&=0\\t\left(V\sin\theta-\frac12gt\right)&=0\end{align*}$$
Since $t\ne0$, $t=\dfrac{2V\sin\theta}{g}$. Then
$$\begin{align*}x&=V\left(\frac{2V\sin\theta}{g}\right)\cos\theta\\&=\frac{V^2(2\sin\theta\cos\theta)}{g}\\&=\frac{V^2\sin2\theta}{g}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Show that if $V^2<100g$ then the horizontal range of the ball is less than $100\text{ m}$.

answer.short: Range $<100\sin2\theta\le100$, so the range is less than $100\text{ m}$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Range}&=\frac{V^2\sin2\theta}{g}\\&<\frac{100g\sin2\theta}{g}\\&=100\sin2\theta\end{align*}$$
Since $\sin2\theta\le1$, $100\sin2\theta\le100$. Therefore the range is less than $100\text{ m}$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: It is now given that $V^2=200g$ and that the horizontal range of the ball is $100\text{ m}$ or more.

spec.description: Axes with the initial velocity vector V drawn from the origin at angle theta to the x-axis, and the horizontal distance of 100 m dimensioned along the x-axis.
spec.mathematics: Launch from the origin with speed V at angle theta to the horizontal; the range required to clear the lake is 100 m. The drawn angle of 45 degrees is illustrative only.
spec.answerVisibility: No trajectory, value of theta or other derived result is shown.

classification.difficultyReason: The student derives the range, solves a trigonometric inequality for the allowed launch angles, and uses that constraint to maximise the projectile's height.

content.prompt:
A particle is projected from a point $O$ with speed $80\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of elevation $\alpha$, where $\tan\alpha=\frac{5}{12}$.
Two seconds later, a second particle is projected from $O$ and it collides with the first particle one second after leaving $O$.
Let $\beta$ be the initial angle of projection for the second projectile.
Let $g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

children.label: i
children.prompt:
Show that the displacement of the first particle after $t$ seconds is given by the equation:
$$\mathbf{s}(t)=80t\cos\alpha\,\mathbf{i}+(80t\sin\alpha-5t^2)\mathbf{j}$$

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\ddot x&=0,\ \dot x=80\cos\alpha,\ x=80t\cos\alpha\\\ddot y&=-10,\ \dot y=80\sin\alpha-10t,\ y=80t\sin\alpha-5t^2\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Find $\tan\beta$.

answer.worked:
$\sin\alpha=\frac5{13}$, $\cos\alpha=\frac{12}{13}$. At collision the first particle has been moving for $3$ s:
$$\mathbf s_1(3)=\frac{2880}{13}\mathbf i+\frac{615}{13}\mathbf j$$The second particle has been moving for $1$ s:
$$\mathbf s_2(1)=V\cos\beta\,\mathbf i+(V\sin\beta-5)\mathbf j$$Equating:
$$V\cos\beta=\frac{2880}{13},\quad V\sin\beta=\frac{615}{13}+5=\frac{680}{13}$$$$\tan\beta=\frac{680}{2880}=\frac{17}{72}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Find the initial velocity of the second particle.

answer.short: $\frac{2880}{13}\mathbf i+\frac{680}{13}\mathbf j\text{ m s}^{-1}$, speed $\approx227.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$
answer.worked:
From part (ii), $V\cos\beta=\frac{2880}{13}$ and $V\sin\beta=\frac{680}{13}$, so the initial velocity is $\frac{2880}{13}\mathbf i+\frac{680}{13}\mathbf j$.
$$V=\sqrt{\left(\frac{2880}{13}\right)^2+\left(\frac{680}{13}\right)^2}\approx227.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Track different elapsed flight times to a common collision, equate position components, and recover the second launch direction and velocity.
