content.prompt:
An object is projected from the origin with an initial velocity of $V$ at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal.
The equations of motion of the object are
$x(t) = Vt \cos \theta$
$y(t) = Vt \sin \theta - \frac{gt^2}{2}$ (Do NOT prove these.)

children.label: i
children.prompt: Show that when the object is projected at an angle $\theta$, the horizontal range is $\frac{V^2}{g}\sin 2\theta$.

answer.short: Range $=\dfrac{V^2}{g}\sin2\theta$. Set $y=0$ for $t>0$, then substitute into $x(t)$.
answer.worked:
The object lands when $y(t)=0$:
$$\begin{align*}0&=t\left(V\sin\theta-\frac{gt}{2}\right)\\t&=\frac{2V\sin\theta}{g}\quad(t>0).\end{align*}$$
Substituting into $x(t)$:
$$\begin{align*}x&=V\left(\frac{2V\sin\theta}{g}\right)\cos\theta\\&=\frac{V^2}{g}\sin2\theta.\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Show that when the object is projected at an angle $\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta$, the horizontal range is also $\frac{V^2}{g}\sin 2\theta$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Range}&=\frac{V^2}{g}\sin\left(2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\right)\\&=\frac{V^2}{g}\sin(\pi-2\theta)\\&=\frac{V^2}{g}\sin2\theta.\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt:
The object is projected with initial velocity $V$ to reach a horizontal distance $d$, which is less than the maximum possible horizontal range.
There are two angles at which the object can be projected in order to travel that horizontal distance before landing.
Let these angles be $\alpha$ and $\beta$, where $\beta=\frac{\pi}{2}-\alpha$.
Let $h_\alpha$ be the maximum height reached by the object when projected at the angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal.
Let $h_\beta$ be the maximum height reached by the object when projected at the angle $\beta$ to the horizontal.
Show that the average of the two heights, $\frac{h_\alpha+h_\beta}{2}$, depends only on $V$ and $g$.

answer.short: $\dfrac{h_\alpha+h_\beta}{2}=\dfrac{V^2}{4g}$, which depends only on $V$ and $g$. Use $h=\dfrac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$ and $\sin\beta=\cos\alpha$.
answer.worked:
Maximum height occurs when $\dot{y}=V\sin\theta-gt=0$, so $t=\dfrac{V\sin\theta}{g}$. Then
$$\begin{align*}h&=\frac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{g}-\frac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}\\&=\frac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}.\end{align*}$$
Since $\beta=\frac{\pi}{2}-\alpha$, $\sin\beta=\cos\alpha$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{h_\alpha+h_\beta}{2}&=\frac12\left(\frac{V^2\sin^2\alpha}{2g}+\frac{V^2\cos^2\alpha}{2g}\right)\\&=\frac{V^2}{4g}(\sin^2\alpha+\cos^2\alpha)\\&=\frac{V^2}{4g}.\end{align*}$$
This depends only on $V$ and $g$.

spec.description: Two projectile paths from the same launch point landing at the same point a distance d away: a high path at angle alpha with maximum height h_alpha and a low path at angle beta with maximum height h_beta. Each has a velocity arrow V, the angles are marked by arcs, and dashed guides and double-headed arrows mark the heights and the range d.
spec.mathematics: Paths y = x tan(theta)(1 - x/d) with alpha + beta = 90 degrees (drawn as 62 and 28 degrees); both land at x = d; h_alpha and h_beta are the peak heights at x = d/2.
spec.answerVisibility: No expressions for the heights or the average are shown.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires deriving the nonzero landing time and range, then independently finding maximum height using zero vertical velocity. The hardest step connects complementary launch angles with the identity sin²α + cos²α = 1 to prove the average height is independent of range.

content.prompt:
A vertical wall, height $H$ metres, stands on horizontal ground.
An object is thrown towards the wall and is projected with an initial speed $u$ m/s at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal plane.
The object is starts from a point on the ground $D$ metres from the wall and it just clears the wall at the highest point of its path.
Let the position of the object at time $t$ be given by $\mathbf{r}(t)$ where
$$\mathbf{r}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}ut\cos\theta \\ ut\sin\theta-\frac{1}{2}gt^2\end{pmatrix}.$$
Do NOT prove this.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Show that the particle reaches the highest point on its path when $t=\frac{u\sin\theta}{g}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\dot y&=u\sin\theta-gt\\0&=u\sin\theta-gt\\t&=\frac{u\sin\theta}{g}\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Show that the speed of projection is given by $u^2=\frac{g}{2H}(4H^2+D^2)$.

answer.worked:
At the top, $x=D$ and $y=H$:
$$\begin{align*}D&=\frac{u^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}\\H&=\frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{g}-\frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}=\frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}\end{align*}$$Dividing, $\frac DH=2\cot\theta$, so $\tan\theta=\frac{2H}{D}$ and $\sin^2\theta=\frac{4H^2}{D^2+4H^2}$.
$$\begin{align*}u^2&=\frac{2gH}{\sin^2\theta}\\&=2gH\cdot\frac{D^2+4H^2}{4H^2}\\&=\frac{g}{2H}(4H^2+D^2)\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt:
Show that $\theta$, the angle of projection, is given by
$$\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2H}{D}\right).$$

answer.worked:
From part (ii), $\frac DH=\frac{u^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/g}{u^2\sin^2\theta/(2g)}=2\cot\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{2H}{D}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2H}{D}\right)\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Relate both coordinates of the highest point to the wall, eliminate the angle to establish the speed formula, and recover the projection angle.

content.prompt:
A particle is projected from the origin at a speed of $10\text{ ms}^{-1}$ and an angle of $\theta$, such that its position after $t$ seconds is given by the vector
$$\mathbf{r}(t)=10t\cos\theta\,\mathbf{i}+(10t\sin\theta-5t^2)\,\mathbf{j}.$$
(Do NOT prove this.)
The ball must pass over a $3\text{ m}$ high vertical wall, whose base is $3\text{ m}$ from the origin.

spec.description: Axes with launch from the origin, initial velocity arrow labelled 10 m/s at angle theta to the horizontal, a dashed line from the origin, and a vertical wall 3 m high with base 3 m from the origin, with both dimensions marked.
spec.mathematics: Wall at x=3, height 3. Directions are schematic; theta is unknown.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied question diagram.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the particle will reach the horizontal position of the wall at $t=\frac{3}{10}\sec\theta$.

answer.worked:
The wall is at $x=3$.
$$\begin{aligned}10t\cos\theta&=3\\t&=\frac{3}{10\cos\theta}\\t&=\frac{3}{10}\sec\theta\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find, to the nearest degree, the range of values of $\theta$ that will allow the particle to pass over the wall.

answer.short: $\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{60-\sqrt{1116}}{18}\right)<\theta<\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{60+\sqrt{1116}}{18}\right)$; the lower and upper endpoints are approximately $56^\circ$ and $79^\circ$, respectively (nearest degree).
answer.worked:
To pass over the wall, the height at $t=\frac{3}{10}\sec\theta$ must exceed $3$.
$$\begin{aligned}10\left(\frac{3}{10}\sec\theta\right)\sin\theta-5\left(\frac{3}{10}\sec\theta\right)^2&>3\\3\tan\theta-\frac{9}{20}\sec^2\theta&>3\\3\tan\theta-\frac{9}{20}(1+\tan^2\theta)&>3\\60\tan\theta-9-9\tan^2\theta&>60\\9\tan^2\theta-60\tan\theta+69&<0\end{aligned}$$
Solving the corresponding quadratic gives the exact roots
$$u_- = \frac{60-\sqrt{1116}}{18}\approx1.4774,\qquad u_+ = \frac{60+\sqrt{1116}}{18}\approx5.1893.$$
The quadratic is negative strictly between its roots, so
$$u_-<\tan\theta<u_+.$$
Hence the exact clearance interval is
$$\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{60-\sqrt{1116}}{18}\right)<\theta<\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{60+\sqrt{1116}}{18}\right).$$
The boundary angles are approximately $55.9075^\circ$ and $79.0925^\circ$, so their values to the nearest degree are approximately $56^\circ$ and $79^\circ$. These are rounded endpoints, not exact strict bounds; $56^\circ$ is in the valid interval.

classification.difficultyReason: The supplied vector and first part scaffold wall time, but the student must translate clearance to a strict inequality, recast it as a quadratic in tan θ, and interpret its interval. That connection is the hardest essential demand.

content.prompt:
From a point $O$ on horizontal ground, a particle $P$ is projected under gravity with speed $V$ in a direction making an angle $\alpha$ with the horizontal.
The particle strikes the ground again at the point $A$.
The equations of motion of $P$ are $x = Vt\cos\alpha$ and $y = -\frac{1}{2}gt^2 + Vt\sin\alpha$. (Do NOT prove these).

children.label: i
children.prompt: Find an expression for the time of flight.

answer.worked:
Let $y=0$:
$$\begin{align*}t\left(V\sin\alpha-\frac12gt\right)&=0\\t&=\frac{2V\sin\alpha}{g}\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Show that the distance $OA = \frac{V^2\sin 2\alpha}{g}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}OA&=V\cos\alpha\cdot\frac{2V\sin\alpha}{g}\\&=\frac{V^2\sin2\alpha}{g}\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt:
At the instant when $P$ is at the highest point of its path, a second particle $Q$ is projected from $O$ with speed $U$ in a direction making an angle $\beta$ with the horizontal.
The particle $Q$ strikes the ground at $A$ at the same instant as $P$.
Given that $\tan \alpha = \frac{4}{3}$, show that $U = \frac{2\sqrt{10}V}{5}$.

answer.worked:
$\sin\alpha=\frac45$, $\cos\alpha=\frac35$, so $OA=\frac{24V^2}{25g}$ and $P$'s flight time is $\frac{8V}{5g}$.
$Q$ is in the air for half of this: $T=\frac{4V}{5g}$.
Horizontal:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{24V^2}{25g}&=U\cos\beta\cdot\frac{4V}{5g}\\U\cos\beta&=\frac{6V}{5}\end{align*}$$Vertical ($y=0$ at $t=T$):
$$\begin{align*}0&=-\frac12g\left(\frac{4V}{5g}\right)^2+U\sin\beta\cdot\frac{4V}{5g}\\U\sin\beta&=\frac{2V}{5}\end{align*}$$$$\begin{align*}U^2&=\frac{36V^2}{25}+\frac{4V^2}{25}=\frac{40V^2}{25}\\U&=\frac{2\sqrt{10}V}{5}\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Use the first projectile's range and half-flight time to determine both components of the second projectile's initial velocity.

content.prompt:
An enemy plane is flying horizontally at height $h$ metres with speed $U\text{ m/s}$.
When it is at point $P$, a ground rocket is fired towards it from the origin $O$ with speed $v\text{ m/s}$ and angle of elevation $\alpha$.
The rocket misses the plane, passing too late through the point $P$.
However, it goes on to reach a maximum height of $3h$ metres and then on its descent strikes the plane at $Q$.
With the axes as shown in the diagram, you may assume that the position vector, $\mathbf{s}$, of the rocket at any time is given by:
$$\mathbf{s}(t)=x(t)\hat{\mathbf{i}}+y(t)\hat{\mathbf{j}},$$
$$x(t)=vt\cos\alpha$$
$$y(t)=-\frac{1}{2}gt^2+vt\sin\alpha$$
where $t$ is the time in seconds after firing and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Show that the initial vertical velocity component $(v\sin\alpha)$ of the rocket's speed equals $\sqrt{6gh}$.

answer.worked:
The maximum height is $\dfrac{(v\sin\alpha)^2}{2g}=3h$.
$$\begin{align*}(v\sin\alpha)^2&=6gh\\v\sin\alpha&=\sqrt{6gh}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt:
If the rocket had not struck the plane at $Q$, it would have returned to the $x$-axis at a distance $d$ metres from $O$.
Show that the horizontal component $(v\cos\alpha)$ of the rocket's speed equals $\frac{gd}{2\sqrt{6gh}}$.

answer.worked:
The time to return to the $x$-axis is
$$T=\frac{2v\sin\alpha}{g}=\frac{2\sqrt{6gh}}{g}.$$
Since the range is $d$:
$$\begin{align*}d&=v\cos\alpha\cdot\frac{2\sqrt{6gh}}{g}\\v\cos\alpha&=\frac{gd}{2\sqrt{6gh}}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt:
Show that the Cartesian equation of the trajectory of the rocket is
$$y=\frac{12hx}{d}\left(1-\frac{x}{d}\right).$$

answer.worked:
Using $t=\dfrac{x}{v\cos\alpha}$:
$$y=x\tan\alpha-\frac{gx^2}{2v^2\cos^2\alpha}.$$
Now
$$\tan\alpha=\frac{\sqrt{6gh}}{\frac{gd}{2\sqrt{6gh}}}=\frac{12h}{d},\qquad \frac{g}{2v^2\cos^2\alpha}=\frac{g}{2\left(\frac{gd}{2\sqrt{6gh}}\right)^2}=\frac{12h}{d^2}.$$
Therefore
$$\begin{align*}y&=\frac{12h}{d}x-\frac{12h}{d^2}x^2\\&=\frac{12hx}{d}\left(1-\frac{x}{d}\right).\end{align*}$$

children.label: iv
children.prompt: If the horizontal component of the rocket's speed is $100(3+\sqrt{6})\text{ m/s}$, find the time taken by the rocket to strike the plane at $Q$, in terms of $d$.

answer.worked:
At $Q$ the plane is at height $h$:
$$\begin{align*}1&=12\frac{x}{d}\left(1-\frac{x}{d}\right)\end{align*}$$
Let $z=\dfrac{x}{d}$.
$$\begin{align*}12z^2-12z+1&=0\\z&=\frac{12\pm\sqrt{96}}{24}\\&=\frac{3\pm\sqrt6}{6}.\end{align*}$$
$Q$ is on the descent, so $x_Q=\dfrac{d(3+\sqrt6)}{6}$. Hence
$$\begin{align*}t_Q&=\frac{x_Q}{v\cos\alpha}\\&=\frac{\frac{d(3+\sqrt6)}{6}}{100(3+\sqrt6)}\\&=\frac{d}{600}\text{ s}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: v
children.prompt: Find the speed of the enemy plane.

answer.worked:
$P$ corresponds to the smaller root, $x_P=\dfrac{d(3-\sqrt6)}{6}$. The plane travels from $P$ to $Q$ in time $\dfrac{d}{600}$.
$$\begin{align*}U&=\frac{x_Q-x_P}{t_Q}\\&=\frac{\frac{d\sqrt6}{3}}{\frac{d}{600}}\\&=200\sqrt6\text{ m/s}.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Parabolic rocket trajectory from the origin, peaking at height 3h and returning to the x-axis at x = d. The horizontal line y = h is the plane's path, with a small aeroplane drawn at P (on the ascent) and at Q (on the descent). Arrows show the rocket's launch velocity V m/s at angle alpha and the plane's velocity U m/s from P.
spec.mathematics: Trajectory y = 12hx/d (1 - x/d), drawn with h = 1.2 and d = 9 (illustrative scale). Maximum 3h at x = d/2. P and Q at x = d(3 -/+ sqrt 6)/6, where y = h.
spec.answerVisibility: No equation, time or speed values are shown. The aeroplanes are simplified editable outline icons centred on P and Q.

classification.difficultyReason: The scaffolded parts lead through a symbolic trajectory, but finding the plane’s speed requires selecting both height intersections and relating their separation to the rocket’s flight time.

content.prompt:
A particle, $P$, is projected from point $A$, which is $147$ m above the ground.
The particle $P$ has an initial speed of $u$ m/s and is projected at an angle of $\theta$ to the horizontal, where $0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}$.
After $T$ seconds, the particle $P$ lands on the ground at point $B$ with a speed of $4u$ m/s.
Acceleration due to gravity is $10$ m/s$^2$.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Find the equations of motion.

answer.short: $\ddot x=0,\ \dot x=u\cos\theta,\ x=ut\cos\theta;\ \ddot y=-10,\ \dot y=u\sin\theta-10t,\ y=147+ut\sin\theta-5t^2$
answer.worked:
Take the origin at ground level below $A$, so the launch point is $(0,147)$.
$$\begin{align*}\ddot x&=0, & \ddot y&=-10\\\dot x&=u\cos\theta, & \dot y&=u\sin\theta-10t\\x&=ut\cos\theta, & y&=147+ut\sin\theta-5t^2\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Find the value of $u$.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Hence, show that $\sin\theta=\frac{5T^2-147}{14T}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}14T\sin\theta&=5T^2-147\\\sin\theta&=\frac{5T^2-147}{14T}\end{align*}$$

children.label: iv
children.prompt: Hence, or otherwise, show that $\frac{\sqrt{735}}{5}<T<7$.

answer.worked:

content.prompt:
A particle is projected from the origin with initial velocity $u \text{ m/s}$ at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal.
The particle lands at $x = R$ on the $x$-axis.
The acceleration vector is given by
$$\mathbf{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -g \end{pmatrix},$$
where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity. (Do NOT prove this.)

children.label: i
children.prompt:
Show that the position vector $\mathbf{r}(t)$ of the particle is given by
$$\mathbf{r}(t) = \begin{pmatrix} ut \cos \theta \\ ut \sin \theta - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 \end{pmatrix}.$$

answer.short:
$\mathbf{r}(t)=ut\cos\theta\mathbf{i}+(ut\sin\theta-\frac12gt^2)\mathbf{j}$.

Integrate twice, using $\mathbf{v}(0)$ and $\mathbf{r}(0)$ for the constants.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\mathbf{v}(t)&=\int\mathbf{a}\,dt=c_1\mathbf{i}+(-gt+c_2)\mathbf{j}.\end{align*}$$
At $t=0$, $\mathbf{v}(0)=u\cos\theta\mathbf{i}+u\sin\theta\mathbf{j}$, so
$$\mathbf{v}(t)=u\cos\theta\mathbf{i}+(u\sin\theta-gt)\mathbf{j}.$$
$$\mathbf{r}(t)=\int\mathbf{v}\,dt=(ut\cos\theta+c_3)\mathbf{i}+(ut\sin\theta-\tfrac12gt^2+c_4)\mathbf{j}.$$
At $t=0$, $\mathbf{r}(0)=\mathbf{0}$, so $c_3=c_4=0$ and
$$\mathbf{r}(t)=ut\cos\theta\mathbf{i}+(ut\sin\theta-\tfrac12gt^2)\mathbf{j}.$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt:
Show that the Cartesian equation of the path of flight is given by
$$y = -\frac{gx^2}{2u^2} \left(\tan^2 \theta - \frac{2u^2}{gx} \tan \theta + 1\right)$$

answer.worked:
From $x=ut\cos\theta$, $t=\dfrac{x}{u\cos\theta}$. Substituting into $y$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=x\tan\theta-\frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}\\&=x\tan\theta-\frac{gx^2}{2u^2}(1+\tan^2\theta)\\&=-\frac{gx^2}{2u^2}\left(\tan^2\theta-\frac{2u^2}{gx}\tan\theta+1\right).\end{align*}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Given $u^2 > gR$, prove that there are 2 distinct values of $\theta$ for which the particle will land at $x = R$.

answer.short: The discriminant of the quadratic in $\tan\theta$ is positive, so there are 2 distinct values of $\theta$. Set $y=0$ at $x=R$ and treat it as a quadratic in $\tan\theta$.
answer.worked:
Landing at $x=R$ means $y=0$:
$$\tan^2\theta-\frac{2u^2}{gR}\tan\theta+1=0.$$
This is a quadratic in $\tan\theta$ with
$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=\left(\frac{2u^2}{gR}\right)^2-4\\&=\frac{4(u^4-g^2R^2)}{g^2R^2}.\end{align*}$$
Since $u^2>gR$, $u^4>g^2R^2$, so $\Delta>0$. There are two distinct values of $\tan\theta$, and since $\tan\theta$ is strictly increasing for $0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}$, two distinct values of $\theta$.

content.prompt:
A small paintball is fired from the origin with initial velocity $14$ metres per second towards an eight-metre high barrier.

The origin is at ground level, $10$ metres from the base of the barrier.

The equations of motion are
$$x=14t\cos\theta$$
$$y=14t\sin\theta-4.9t^2$$
where $\theta$ is the angle to the horizontal at which the paintball is fired and $t$ is the time in seconds. (Do NOT prove these equations of motion.)

children.label: i
children.prompt: Show that the equation of trajectory of the paintball is $y=mx-\left(\dfrac{1+m^2}{40}\right)x^2$, where $m=\tan\theta$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}t&=\frac{x}{14\cos\theta}\\y&=14\left(\frac{x}{14\cos\theta}\right)\sin\theta-4.9\left(\frac{x}{14\cos\theta}\right)^2\\&=x\tan\theta-\frac{x^2}{40}\sec^2\theta\\&=x\tan\theta-\frac{x^2}{40}(1+\tan^2\theta)\end{align*}$$
Let $m=\tan\theta$:
$$y=mx-\left(\frac{1+m^2}{40}\right)x^2.$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt:
Show that the paintball hits the barrier at height $h$ metres when $m=2\pm\sqrt{3-0.4h}$.

Hence determine the maximum value of $h$.

answer.short:
$h_{\max}=7.5\text{ m}$

Substitute $x=10$, $y=h$ to get a quadratic in $m$; real solutions need a non-negative discriminant.
answer.worked:
At the barrier, $x=10$ and $y=h$:
$$\begin{align*}h&=10m-2.5(1+m^2)\\2.5m^2-10m+(2.5+h)&=0\\m&=\frac{10\pm\sqrt{100-10(2.5+h)}}{5}\\&=\frac{10\pm5\sqrt{3-0.4h}}{5}\\&=2\pm\sqrt{3-0.4h}\end{align*}$$
For real $m$:
$$\begin{align*}3-0.4h&\ge0\\h&\le7.5\end{align*}$$
The maximum value of $h$ is $7.5$ m.

children.label: iii
children.prompt:
There is a large hole in the barrier.

The bottom of the hole is $3.9$ metres above the ground and the top of the hole is $5.9$ metres above the ground.

The paintball passes through the hole if $m$ is in one of two intervals.

One interval is $2.8\le m\le3.2$.

Find the other interval.

answer.worked:
When $h=5.9$:
$$m=2\pm\sqrt{0.64}=2\pm0.8,$$ so $m=2.8$ or $1.2$.

When $h=3.9$:
$$m=2\pm\sqrt{1.44}=2\pm1.2,$$ so $m=3.2$ or $0.8$.

The other interval is $0.8\le m\le1.2$.

children.label: iv
children.prompt:
Show that, if the paintball passes through the hole, the range is $\dfrac{40m}{1+m^2}$ metres.

Hence find the widths of the two intervals in which the paintball can land at ground level on the other side of the barrier.

answer.short:
Range $=\dfrac{40m}{1+m^2}$ m. The widths are $\approx1.28\text{ m}$ and $\approx0.49\text{ m}$.

For $0.8\le m\le1.2$ the range peaks at $20$ m when $m=1$; the least range is $19.51$ m at $m=0.8$ (at $m=1.2$ it is $19.67$ m).
answer.worked:
Set $y=0$ with $x>0$:
$$\begin{align*}mx-\left(\frac{1+m^2}{40}\right)x^2&=0\\x&=\frac{40m}{1+m^2}\end{align*}$$
For $2.8\le m\le3.2$:
$$\begin{align*}m=2.8:\ x&=\frac{112}{8.84}\approx12.67\\m=3.2:\ x&=\frac{128}{11.24}\approx11.39\\\text{width}&\approx12.67-11.39\\&\approx1.28\text{ m}\end{align*}$$
For $0.8\le m\le1.2$, compare both endpoints and the peak at $m=1$:
$$\begin{align*}m=0.8:\ x&=\frac{32}{1.64}\approx19.51\\m=1.2:\ x&=\frac{48}{2.44}\approx19.67\\m=1:\ x&=\frac{40}{2}=20\end{align*}$$
The range is greatest at $m=1$ and least at $m=0.8$, so the landing interval is $19.51\le x\le20$:
$$\begin{align*}\text{width}&\approx20-19.51\\&\approx0.49\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A particle is projected from the origin with initial speed $V$ at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal.

You may assume the equation of its parabolic path is $y=x\tan\theta-\dfrac{gx^2\sec^2\theta}{2V^2}$. Use $g=10\text{ m/s}^2$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, and hence show that the vertex of the parabola is $\left(\dfrac{V^2\sin 2\theta}{2g},\dfrac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}\right)$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{dy}{dx}&=\tan\theta-\frac{gx\sec^2\theta}{V^2}.\end{align*}$$
At the vertex, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta-\frac{gx\sec^2\theta}{V^2}&=0\\x&=\frac{V^2\tan\theta}{g\sec^2\theta}\\x&=\frac{V^2\sin 2\theta}{2g}.\end{align*}$$
Substitute into the equation for $y$:
$$\begin{align*}y_{\text{vertex}}&=\frac{V^2\sin 2\theta}{2g}\tan\theta-\left(\frac{V^2\sin 2\theta}{2g}\right)^2\frac{g\sec^2\theta}{2V^2}\\y_{\text{vertex}}&=\frac{V^2\cdot2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{2g}\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}-\frac{V^4\cdot4\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta}{4g^2}\frac{g}{2V^2\cos^2\theta}\\y_{\text{vertex}}&=\frac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{g}-\frac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}\\y_{\text{vertex}}&=\frac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}.\end{align*}$$
Hence the vertex is $\left(\dfrac{V^2\sin 2\theta}{2g},\dfrac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}\right)$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If $V=20\text{ m/s}$ and the greatest height is $15\text{ m}$, find $\theta$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\frac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}&=15\\\frac{400\sin^2\theta}{20}&=15\\\sin^2\theta&=\frac34\\\sin\theta&=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\\theta&=60^\circ.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A particle is projected from level ground with initial speed $V$ m/s at an angle of $\theta$ to the horizontal.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that:

children.label: i
children.prompt: the greatest height is $\dfrac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$ metres,

answer.worked:
At greatest height, $\dot y=0$:
$$\begin{align*}V\sin\theta-gt&=0\\t&=\frac{V\sin\theta}{g}.\end{align*}$$
Substituting into $y=Vt\sin\theta-\frac12gt^2$:
$$\begin{align*}H&=V\sin\theta\cdot\frac{V\sin\theta}{g}-\frac12g\left(\frac{V\sin\theta}{g}\right)^2\\H&=\frac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{g}-\frac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}\\H&=\frac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}\text{ metres}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: the horizontal range is $\dfrac{V^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$ metres.

answer.worked:
The particle lands when $y=0$:
$$\begin{align*}V\sin\theta\cdot t-\frac12gt^2&=0\\t\left(V\sin\theta-\frac12gt\right)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Taking the positive landing time,
$$t=\frac{2V\sin\theta}{g}.$$
Hence
$$\begin{align*}R&=V\cos\theta\cdot\frac{2V\sin\theta}{g}\\R&=\frac{V^2(2\sin\theta\cos\theta)}{g}\\R&=\frac{V^2\sin 2\theta}{g}\text{ metres}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: If the horizontal range is five times the greatest height, prove that $\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac45\right)$.

answer.worked:
Using $R=5H$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{V^2\sin 2\theta}{g}&=5\cdot\frac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}\\2\sin\theta\cos\theta&=\frac52\sin^2\theta.\end{align*}$$
Divide both sides by $\sin\theta$, where $\sin\theta\ne0$:
$$\begin{align*}2\cos\theta&=\frac52\sin\theta\\\tan\theta&=\frac45\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac45\right).\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: By rewriting $y=-\dfrac{gx^2}{2V^2}(1+\tan^2\theta)+x\tan\theta$ as a quadratic in $\tan\theta$, show that a projectile can pass through the point $P(x,y)$ only if $y\le\dfrac{V^4-g^2x^2}{2V^2g}$ and explain what this means geometrically.

answer.short: $gx^2\tan^2\theta-2V^2x\tan\theta+2V^2y+gx^2=0$. Real launch angles require $\Delta\ge0$, giving $y\le\dfrac{V^4-g^2x^2}{2gV^2}$. Reachable points lie on or below this parabola; points above it cannot be reached.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}y&=-\frac{gx^2}{2V^2}-\frac{gx^2}{2V^2}\tan^2\theta+x\tan\theta\\2V^2y&=-gx^2-gx^2\tan^2\theta+2V^2x\tan\theta\\gx^2\tan^2\theta-2V^2x\tan\theta+2V^2y+gx^2&=0.\end{align*}$$

For $x\ne0$, this quadratic in $\tan\theta$ must have a real solution. Hence $\Delta\ge0$:

$$\begin{align*}(-2V^2x)^2-4(gx^2)(2V^2y+gx^2)&\ge0\\4V^4x^2-8gx^2V^2y-4g^2x^4&\ge0\\-8gx^2V^2y&\ge-4V^4x^2+4g^2x^4\\y&\le\frac{-4V^4x^2+4g^2x^4}{-8gx^2V^2}\\y&\le\frac{V^4-g^2x^2}{2gV^2}.\end{align*}$$

Dividing the inequality by $-8gx^2V^2$ reverses its direction. In the final fraction, divide the numerator and denominator by $-4x^2$.

For $x=0$, vertical projection reaches a maximum height of $\dfrac{V^2}{2g}$, consistent with the same boundary.

All points on or below the parabola $y=\dfrac{V^4-g^2x^2}{2gV^2}$ can be reached by choosing a suitable launch angle $\theta$. Points above it cannot be reached because no real launch angle exists.

entries.description: Projectile Motion and Velocity as a Vector

A projectile is an object dropped, thrown, struck, or fired into the air near Earth's surface.
We model a projectile as a single point.
The only force acting on a projectile is gravity. We ignore air resistance.
There is only vertical acceleration downwards, and no horizontal acceleration.

entries.description: Projectile Motion as Vectors

body: In Year 11, you studied motion in a straight line. Here, we extend this to projectile motion in two dimensions.
The displacement of a projectile traces a parabolic curve.
The velocity vector at any point is tangent to the path. The direction of travel is therefore dy/dx.
We can resolve each velocity vector into horizontal and vertical components.
The horizontal and vertical components are independent; they have no effect on each other.

entries.description: Deriving the Six Equations of Motion

The three equations of motion in one dimension describe displacement, velocity, and acceleration with respect to time t, related by differentiation and integration.

x(t): displacement     ẋ(t): velocity     ẍ: acceleration

In projectile motion, there are six equations of motion:
three for horizontal motion and three for vertical motion.
Every projectile motion problem starts from two facts:
• ẍ(t) = 0     No horizontal force acts, so there is no horizontal acceleration.
• ÿ(t) = −g     The only vertical force is the constant force of gravity.

The remaining four equations follow by integrating these twice.

entries.description: Using the Equations of Motion

Maximum Height is where \(\dot y=0\)
A projectile rises, reaches a maximum height, then falls.
Vertical velocity is positive while rising and negative while falling,
At the maximum height, where the motion changes direction, the vertical velocity is zero.
To find the maximum height, set \(\dot y(t)=0\) to find the time at which the projectile reaches maximum height, then substitute into \(y(t)\).

Projectile lands when \(y=0\)
For a projectile launched from ground level, it lands when it returns to ground level, \(y(t)=0\).
Setting \(y(t)=0\) gives two solutions: \(t=0\) (launch) and a \(t=\) positive value (landing).
The time of landing is also called the time of flight.

entries.description:
Cartesian Equation of Projectile Motion
\[y=-\frac{gx^2}{2V^2}\sec^2\theta+x\tan\theta\]
\[y=-\frac{gx^2}{2V^2}(1+\tan^2\theta)+x\tan\theta\]
Do not memorise these equations. They will either be given, or you will need to derive them.
The Cartesian equation can be very useful as it relates x and y directly:
• The instantaneous direction of the projectile is given by \(\tan\phi=\frac{dy}{dx}\).
• The range is given by setting \(y=0\).
• The maximum height can be found by setting \(\frac{dy}{dx}=0\), or by using \(x=-\frac{b}{2a}\).

entries.description: Suppose V = 200 m/s and the shell hits a target 3 km horizontally and 0.5 km vertically from the gun. Show that tan α = (4 + √3)/3 or tan α = (4 − √3)/3, and hence find the two possible values of α to the nearest minute.

entries.description:
From x = Vt cos α: t = x/(V cos α); sub into y:
y = −(g/2)(x/(V cos α))² + Vx sin α/(V cos α)
= x tan α − gx²sec²α/(2V²)
Rearrange: (gx²/(2V²))(1 + tan²α) − x tan α + y = 0; multiply by 2V²:
gx²tan²α − 2xV²tan α + (2yV² + gx²) = 0.

With the Cartesian equation, we can derive the general equation for the range of a projectile.
Using y = −(gx²/(2V²))sec²θ + x tan θ, show, using the properties of the sine graph, that the range of an object projected from ground level is x = (V²/g)sin 2θ, and explain why the maximum range occurs at an angle of projection of 45°.

entries.description: Supplied blue solution, labelled a) and b).
entries.expectedAnswer:
a) y = 0, x ≠ 0:
x tan θ = (gx²/(2V²))sec²θ
x = (2V² tan θ)/(g sec²θ)
  = (2V² sin θ cos θ)/g
  = (V² sin 2θ)/g

b) −1 ≤ sin 2θ ≤ 1
∴ max range = V²/g
sin 2θ = 1 at 2θ = 90°
θ = 45°

entries.description: By rewriting y = −(gx²/(2V²))(1 + tan²θ) + x tan θ as a quadratic in tan θ, show that a projectile can pass through the point P(x, y) only if y ≤ (V⁴ − g²x²)/(2V²g) and explain what this means geometrically.
entries.presentation: Black question text followed by an open working region.

entries.description: Supplied blue algebraic working and geometric explanation. Transcription below retains the source error in its third line.
entries.expectedAnswer:
y = −gx²/(2V²) + (−gx²/(2V²))tan²θ + x tan θ
2V²y = −gx² − gx²tan²θ + 2V²x tan θ
gx²tan θ − 2V²x tan θ + 2V²y + gx² = 0

For this equation to be true, there must be real values of θ that satisfy it.
In other words, Δ ≥ 0

(−2V²x)² − 4(gx²)(2V²y + gx²) ≥ 0
4V⁴x² − 8gx²V²y − 4g²x⁴ ≥ 0
−8gx²V²y ≥ −4V⁴x² + 4g²x⁴
y ≤ (−4V⁴x² + 4g²x⁴)/(−8gx²V²), with numerator and denominator divided by −4x²
y ≤ (V⁴ − g²x²)/(2gV²)

This means all points on or below the parabola y = (V⁴ − g²x²)/(2gV²) can be reached by some variable launch angle θ.
Points above it cannot be reached because no real launch angle exists.

entries.description: We can resolve each velocity vector into horizontal and vertical components. The horizontal and vertical components are independent; they have no effect on each other.

body: In Year 11, you studied motion in a straight line. Here, we extend this to projectile motion in two dimensions.
The displacement of a projectile traces a parabolic curve.
The velocity vector at any point is tangent to the path. The direction of travel is therefore dy/dx.
We can resolve each velocity vector into horizontal and vertical components.
The horizontal and vertical components are independent; they have no effect on each other.
